questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting phenotype numbers from crosses showing incomplete dominance (snapdragon flower colour) and co-dominance (AB blood group), where genotype and phenotype ratios coincide
questions.question: In snapdragon, RR plants are red, Rr pink and rr white. (i) Two pink plants are crossed and 240 seedlings raised. (ii) A pink plant is crossed with a white one and 120 seedlings raised. (iii) Two persons of blood group AB (IᴬIᴮ) have children. Which set of expected results is correct?
options: A) (i) 180 red : 60 white; (ii) all pink; (iii) all AB
B) (i) 60 red : 120 pink : 60 white; (ii) 60 red : 60 white; (iii) A and B only, 1 : 1

C) (i) 60 red : 120 pink : 60 white; (ii) 60 pink : 60 white; (iii) A : AB : B = 1 : 2 : 1 — in both incomplete dominance and co-dominance the heterozygote has its own phenotype, so the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio
D) (i) 120 red : 120 white; (ii) 120 pink; (iii) A : B : AB : O = 1 : 1 : 1 : 1
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 60 : 120 : 60; 60 pink : 60 white; A : AB : B = 1 : 2 : 1.
Concept: In incomplete dominance the F₁ has a phenotype that does not resemble either of the two parents and is in between the two, as in the inheritance of flower colour in the dog flower (snapdragon, Antirrhinum sp.): in a cross between true-breeding red (RR) and white (rr), the F₁ (Rr) is pink, and on self-pollination the F₂ ratio is 1 (RR) red : 2 (Rr) pink : 1 (rr) white, so the genotypic ratio is exactly like any Mendelian monohybrid cross but the phenotypic ratio has changed from 3 : 1 to 1 : 2 : 1. In co-dominance the F₁ generation resembles both parents, as in the ABO blood groups, where Iᴬ and Iᴮ are both expressed when present together, giving blood group AB.
Given: (i) Rr × Rr, 240 seedlings; (ii) Rr × rr, 120 seedlings; (iii) IᴬIᴮ × IᴬIᴮ.
Formula/Principle: Monohybrid segregation; each heterozygote distinguishable.
Step 1: (i) RR : Rr : rr = 1 : 2 : 1 ⇒ 60 red, 120 pink, 60 white.
Step 2: (ii) Rr × rr ⇒ Rr : rr = 1 : 1 ⇒ 60 pink, 60 white.
Step 3: (iii) IᴬIᴬ : IᴬIᴮ : IᴮIᴮ = 1 : 2 : 1 ⇒ A : AB : B = 1 : 2 : 1.
Why: Because neither allele masks the other, every genotype has its own phenotype, so phenotypes can be counted directly as genotypes.
Why not the others: (A) Assumes complete dominance with wrong ratios. (B) Pink × white cannot give red; AB × AB gives AB children too. (D) Ratios wrong; O needs an i allele, absent here.
Key point: Incomplete dominance and co-dominance: phenotypic ratio = genotypic ratio (1 : 2 : 1).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: How the I gene's three alleles produce the ABO blood groups through sugar addition to the cell surface, predicting children's groups, and pleiotropy in phenylketonuria
questions.question: The ABO blood groups are controlled by gene I with alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i. A man of group A whose mother was group O marries a woman of group B whose father was group O. Which reasoning is correct?
options: A) Iᴬ and Iᴮ produce slightly different forms of a sugar polymer on the red cell surface, while i produces none; the man must be Iᴬi and the woman Iᴮi, so each child has a 1/4 chance of each group A, B, AB and O; six genotypes are possible in the population with three alleles; phenylketonuria shows pleiotropy, a single mutant gene causing mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation
B) The man is IᴬIᴬ, so no child can be group O
C) Their children can only be A or B, because AB requires both parents to be AB
D) With three alleles, only three genotypes are possible
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Iᴬi × Iᴮi gives A, B, AB and O, each 1/4; six genotypes; PKU illustrates pleiotropy.
Concept: ABO blood groups are controlled by the gene I. The plasma membrane of the red blood cells has sugar polymers that protrude from its surface, and the kind of sugar is controlled by the gene. The gene has three alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i; Iᴬ and Iᴮ produce a slightly different form of the sugar while allele i does not produce any sugar. Because humans are diploid, each person possesses any two of the three I gene alleles; Iᴬ and Iᴮ are completely dominant over i, but when Iᴬ and Iᴮ are present together they both express their own types of sugars (co-dominance). Since there are three different alleles, there are six different combinations and therefore six different genotypes of human ABO blood types. Pleiotropy is when a single gene exhibits multiple phenotypic expressions, as in phenylketonuria, caused by mutation in the gene coding for the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, whose patients show mental retardation and reduction in hair and skin pigmentation.
Step 1: The man is group A with an O mother, who could only pass i ⇒ man Iᴬi.
Step 2: The woman is group B with an O father ⇒ woman Iᴮi.
Step 3: Iᴬi × Iᴮi ⇒ IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B), ii (O), each 1/4.
Why: The pedigree fixes the hidden recessive allele in each parent; the enzyme-and-sugar mechanism explains why i is recessive and Iᴬ, Iᴮ co-dominant.
Why not the others: (B) The O mother forces the man to carry i. (C) Iᴬ from one parent and Iᴮ from the other give AB. (D) Three alleles give six genotypes.
Key point: Gene I: Iᴬ = Iᴮ > i; six genotypes, four blood groups; PKU = pleiotropy.

questions.sub_topic: The order in which DNA is packaged in a eukaryotic nucleus, from nucleosome to chromosome, the role of histones and NHC proteins, and euchromatin versus heterochromatin
questions.question: Which sequence and description of DNA packaging in a eukaryotic nucleus is correct?
options: A) DNA first folds into chromosomes, which then wrap round histones to form nucleosomes; heterochromatin is lightly stained and transcriptionally active
B) Histones are negatively charged proteins rich in glutamate and aspartate, which bind the negatively charged DNA directly
C) Nucleosomes are formed by RNA wrapped round histone octamers

D) Negatively charged DNA wraps round a positively charged histone octamer (histones are rich in lysine and arginine) to form a nucleosome of about 200 bp; nucleosomes form the "beads-on-string" structure seen in chromatin, which is coiled further into chromatin fibres and, at metaphase, condensed into chromosomes, the higher-level packaging requiring non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins; loosely packed, lightly stained euchromatin is transcriptionally active, while densely packed, dark-stained heterochromatin is inactive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) DNA + histone octamer → nucleosome → beads-on-string → chromatin fibre → chromosome; NHC proteins; euchromatin active, heterochromatin inactive.
Concept: In eukaryotes there is a set of positively charged, basic proteins called histones; a protein acquires charge depending upon the abundance of amino acid residues with charged side chains, and histones are rich in the basic amino acid residues lysine and arginine, both of which carry positive charges in their side chains. Histones are organised to form a unit of eight molecules called the histone octamer. The negatively charged DNA is wrapped around the positively charged histone octamer to form a structure called the nucleosome; a typical nucleosome contains 200 bp of DNA helix. Nucleosomes constitute the repeating unit of a structure in the nucleus called chromatin, thread-like stained bodies seen as "beads-on-string" under the electron microscope. The beads-on-string structure in chromatin is packaged to form chromatin fibres that are further coiled and condensed at metaphase stage of cell division to form chromosomes. The packaging of chromatin at a higher level requires an additional set of proteins collectively referred to as non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins. In a typical nucleus, some regions of chromatin are loosely packed and stain light (euchromatin) and are transcriptionally active; others are densely packed and stain dark (heterochromatin) and are inactive.
Step 1: Charge attraction: DNA (phosphate, −) + histone octamer (lysine, arginine, +) ⇒ nucleosome.
Step 2: Nucleosomes in series ⇒ beads-on-string chromatin ⇒ chromatin fibre.
Step 3: Further coiling with NHC proteins ⇒ metaphase chromosome.
Why: Packaging must neutralise the repulsion between phosphate groups, which positively charged histones do, before any higher folding is possible.
Why not the others: (A) Order reversed and euchromatin/heterochromatin swapped. (B) Histones are basic (positive). (C) Nucleosomes contain DNA.
Key point: Nucleosome (≈200 bp DNA + histone octamer) → chromatin → chromosome; euchromatin active.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the Meselson–Stahl ¹⁵N/¹⁴N density experiment generation by generation, and the enzymes and direction of synthesis at the replication fork
questions.question: E. coli grown for many generations in ¹⁵NH₄Cl is transferred to ¹⁴NH₄Cl, and DNA is extracted after each generation (about 20 min) and centrifuged in a CsCl density gradient. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) After one generation two bands appear, one heavy and one light, proving semiconservative replication

B) After one generation all DNA forms a single band of intermediate (hybrid) density, and after two generations equal amounts of hybrid and light DNA appear — exactly as predicted if each daughter molecule keeps one parental strand (semiconservative replication); at the fork DNA polymerase synthesises new strands only in the 5′→3′ direction, so one strand is made continuously and the other discontinuously as Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase, beginning at a defined origin of replication
C) After two generations all DNA is of intermediate density
D) The result shows conservative replication, since heavy DNA disappears
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Generation 1: all hybrid; generation 2: half hybrid, half light; polymerase works 5′→3′, lagging strand in Okazaki fragments joined by ligase.
Concept: Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl grew E. coli in a medium containing ¹⁵NH₄Cl (¹⁵N being the heavy isotope of nitrogen) as the only nitrogen source for many generations, so ¹⁵N was incorporated into newly synthesised DNA. The heavy DNA can be distinguished from normal DNA by centrifugation in a caesium chloride density gradient. They then transferred the cells into a medium with normal ¹⁴NH₄Cl and took samples at definite time intervals as the cells multiplied. The DNA extracted from the culture one generation after the transfer (i.e. after 20 minutes; E. coli divides in 20 minutes) had a hybrid or intermediate density; DNA extracted after another generation (after 40 minutes) was composed of equal amounts of this hybrid DNA and of light DNA. The main enzyme of replication is DNA-dependent DNA polymerase, which catalyses polymerisation only in one direction, 5′→3′; consequently, on one strand (template with polarity 3′→5′) replication is continuous, while on the other it is discontinuous, and the discontinuously synthesised fragments are later joined by the enzyme DNA ligase. Replication originates at a definite region of E. coli DNA called the origin of replication.
Given: ¹⁵N/¹⁵N parental DNA; growth in ¹⁴N.
Step 1: Generation 1: each molecule = one ¹⁵N strand + one ¹⁴N strand ⇒ single hybrid band.
Step 2: Generation 2: hybrid molecules give 1 hybrid + 1 light each ⇒ 50 % hybrid, 50 % light.
Step 3: Conservative replication would have given heavy + light bands after generation 1, which was not seen.
Why: Each parental strand serves as a template and stays paired with its new complementary strand.
Why not the others: (A) That is the conservative prediction. (C) Light DNA appears in the second generation. (D) The hybrid band rules out conservative replication.
Key point: Meselson–Stahl: hybrid in generation 1, hybrid + light in generation 2 ⇒ semiconservative.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of events from the formation of the Earth to the appearance of the first life forms according to the chemical theory of the origin of life
questions.question: Which sequence of events in the origin of life on Earth is correct?
options: A) The Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago with no atmosphere at first; water vapour, methane, carbon dioxide and ammonia released from the molten mass covered the surface; UV rays split water into hydrogen and oxygen, and oxygen combined with ammonia and methane to form water, CO₂ and other gases, while the ozone layer formed; as the Earth cooled, water vapour fell as rain to fill the oceans; organic molecules formed by chemical evolution, and the first non-cellular forms of life appeared about 3 billion years ago, followed by single-celled organisms in water
B) Cells appeared first, and they then made the organic molecules and the atmosphere
C) Life arose 4.5 billion years ago from spores that came from other planets, and oceans formed later
D) Oxygen-rich air was present from the start, allowing aerobic cells to form immediately
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Earth → gases from molten mass → UV splitting of water, ozone → oceans → organic molecules → non-cellular life (~3 bya) → unicellular organisms.
Concept: Earth was formed about 4.5 billion years back. There was no atmosphere on early Earth; water vapour, methane, carbon dioxide and ammonia released from the molten mass covered the surface. The UV rays from the sun broke up water into hydrogen and oxygen, and the lighter H₂ escaped; oxygen combined with ammonia and methane to form water, CO₂ and others, and the ozone layer was formed. As it cooled, the water vapour fell as rain to fill the depressions and form oceans. Life appeared 500 million years after the formation of the Earth, i.e. almost four billion years back. The first non-cellular forms of life could have originated 3 billion years back; they would have been giant molecules (RNA, protein, polysaccharides etc.), and these capsules reproduced their molecules perhaps; the first cellular form of life did not originate till about 2000 million years ago, and these were probably single cells, all life forms being in the water environment only.
Step 1: Physical events: formation of Earth → outgassing → UV chemistry and ozone → oceans.
Step 2: Chemical evolution: simple inorganic molecules → organic molecules (e.g. amino acids) in the oceans.
Step 3: Biological evolution: non-cellular aggregates → single cells in water.
Why: Chemical evolution needs a reducing environment and water; cells could form only after their building blocks accumulated.
Why not the others: (B) Molecules preceded cells. (C) Panspermia is not the accepted sequence, and oceans preceded life. (D) The early atmosphere lacked free oxygen.
Key point: Earth (4.5 bya) → oceans → chemical evolution → non-cellular life → cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing methods of cancer detection (biopsy, radiography, CT, MRI, antibody tests) and of treatment (surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy), and classes of carcinogens
questions.question: Which comparison about the detection and treatment of cancer is correct?
options: A) MRI uses ionising X-rays, while CT uses strong magnetic fields; α-interferon kills cancer cells directly like a cytotoxic drug
B) Biopsy uses radioactive tracers; chemotherapy has no side effects

C) Biopsy with histopathological study confirms cancer from a piece of the suspected tissue; CT uses X-rays to generate a three-dimensional image of internal organs, whereas MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation to detect pathological and physiological changes in living tissue; radiotherapy kills tumour cells while taking care of the surrounding normal tissue, most chemotherapeutic drugs cause side effects such as hair loss and anaemia, and biological response modifiers such as α-interferon activate the immune system to destroy the tumour; carcinogens include ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays), non-ionising radiation (UV), chemicals (tobacco smoke) and oncogenic viruses
D) All tumours are malignant; UV is ionising radiation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Biopsy/histopathology confirms; CT = X-rays, MRI = magnetic fields, non-ionising; radiotherapy, chemotherapy (side effects), immunotherapy (α-interferon).
Concept: Cancer detection is based on biopsy and histopathological studies of the tissue and blood and bone marrow tests for increased cell counts in the case of leukemias; in biopsy, a piece of the suspected tissue cut into thin sections is stained and examined under the microscope (histopathological studies) by a pathologist. Techniques like radiography (use of X-rays), CT (computed tomography) and MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) are very useful to detect cancers of internal organs; CT uses X-rays to generate a three-dimensional image of the internals of an object, while MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations to accurately detect pathological and physiological changes in living tissue. Antibodies against cancer-specific antigens are also used. Treatment: in surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy, tumour cells are removed or killed; in radiotherapy, tumour cells are irradiated lethally, taking proper care of the normal tissues surrounding the tumour mass; several chemotherapeutic drugs are used, and the majority of them have side effects like hair loss, anaemia, etc. Tumour cells avoid detection and destruction by the immune system, so patients are given substances called biological response modifiers such as α-interferon, which activates their immune system and helps in destroying the tumour. Transformation of normal cells into cancerous neoplastic cells may be induced by physical, chemical or biological agents called carcinogens; ionising radiations like X-rays and gamma rays and non-ionising radiations like UV cause DNA damage, the chemical carcinogens present in tobacco smoke have been identified as a major cause of lung cancer, and cancer-causing viruses called oncogenic viruses have genes called viral oncogenes.
Why: Each detection method samples a different property (cell structure, X-ray absorption, magnetic response of tissue), and each treatment acts at a different level (removal, DNA damage, immune activation).
Why not the others: (A) CT and MRI swapped; α-interferon works through the immune system. (B) Biopsy is a tissue sample; chemotherapy has side effects. (D) Benign tumours exist; UV is non-ionising.
Key point: CT (X-rays) vs MRI (magnetic, non-ionising); α-interferon activates immunity.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Choosing a suitable cloning vector from a table of plasmid features: origin of replication, selectable marker and number of recognition sites for the restriction enzyme
questions.question:
Four plasmids are compared for cloning a gene cut out with EcoRI.

Plasmid | Origin of replication (ori) | Selectable marker | EcoRI recognition sites
P | absent | ampicillin resistance | 1
Q | present | ampicillin resistance | 1
R | present | none | 1
S | present | ampicillin resistance | 3

Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) S is best, because more EcoRI sites allow more copies of the gene to be inserted

B) Q is the suitable vector: its ori lets it replicate and controls copy number inside the host; its antibiotic-resistance gene allows transformants to be selected on ampicillin medium while non-transformants die; and a single EcoRI site means cutting opens the plasmid at one place only — P cannot replicate in the host, R gives no way to pick out transformed cells, and S would be cut into several fragments
C) R is best, because selectable markers are harmful to the host
D) P is best, because without ori the foreign gene will be copied more often
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Plasmid Q — ori, selectable marker and a single recognition site.
Concept: Features required to facilitate cloning into a vector: (i) Origin of replication (ori): the sequence from where replication starts; any piece of DNA linked to this sequence can be made to replicate within the host cells, and this sequence is also responsible for controlling the copy number of the linked DNA. (ii) Selectable marker: the vector requires a selectable marker which helps in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of the transformants; normally the genes encoding resistance to antibiotics such as ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin are considered useful selectable markers for E. coli. (iii) Cloning sites: in order to link the alien DNA, the vector needs to have very few, preferably single, recognition sites for the commonly used restriction enzymes; the presence of more than one recognition site within the vector will generate several fragments, which will complicate gene cloning.
Given: Table of features of P, Q, R, S.
Step 1: Without ori (P), the plasmid and its insert cannot replicate in the host.
Step 2: Without a marker (R), transformed cells cannot be selected from the vast majority of untransformed ones.
Step 3: Three EcoRI sites (S) cut the plasmid into three fragments; only Q satisfies all three requirements.
Why: Transformation is inefficient, so a selection method is essential; replication needs ori; a unique site preserves the vector's integrity.
Why not the others: (A) Multiple sites fragment the vector. (C) Markers are needed for selection. (D) Without ori there is no replication at all.
Key point: Vector needs ori, a selectable marker and a unique cloning site.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating change in population size, birth rate and death rate from natality, mortality, immigration and emigration, and reading the shape of an age pyramid
questions.question: A deer population of 500 records, in one year, 100 births, 60 deaths, 20 immigrants and 10 emigrants. Its age pyramid has a broad base of pre-reproductive individuals. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) Size next year 530; birth rate 0.2; the pyramid shows a declining population
B) Size next year 550; birth rate 100 per year; death rate 60 per year; the pyramid is bell-shaped (stable)
C) Size next year 610; birth rate 0.12; the pyramid shows a stable population

D) Size next year 500 + (100 + 20) − (60 + 10) = 550; birth rate = 100/500 = 0.2 per individual per year and death rate = 60/500 = 0.12 per individual per year; a broad-based (triangular) age pyramid indicates an expanding (growing) population
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 550; birth rate 0.2, death rate 0.12 per individual per year; expanding population.
Concept: A population has certain attributes that an individual organism does not: birth rates and death rates; in a population these rates refer to per capita births and deaths, respectively, expressed as change in numbers (increase or decrease) with respect to members of the population. The size of a population for any species is not static; it fluctuates depending on four basic processes, two of which (natality and immigration) contribute an increase in population density and two (mortality and emigration) a decrease: Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + [(B + I) − (D + E)]. If the age distribution (per cent individuals of a given age or age group) is plotted for the population, the resulting structure is called an age pyramid; the shape of the pyramid reflects the growth status of the population — whether it is growing (triangular, broad base), stable (bell-shaped) or declining (urn-shaped).
Given: N = 500, B = 100, D = 60, I = 20, E = 10.
Formula/Principle: Nₜ₊₁ = Nₜ + (B + I) − (D + E); rate = number/N.
Step 1: Nₜ₊₁ = 500 + 120 − 70 = 550.
Step 2: Birth rate = 100/500 = 0.2; death rate = 60/500 = 0.12.
Step 3: Broad pre-reproductive base ⇒ more individuals entering reproductive age ⇒ expanding.
Why: Per capita rates allow comparison between populations of different sizes; the base of the pyramid predicts future reproduction.
Why not the others: (A) Arithmetic and pyramid reading wrong. (B) Rates must be per capita; a broad base is triangular, not bell-shaped. (C) Wrong size and rates.
Key point: N(t+1) = N + B + I − D − E; per capita rates; broad base = expanding.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why ecological pyramids of number and biomass can be inverted while the pyramid of energy is always upright, and the limitations of the pyramid concept
questions.question: Which explanation about ecological pyramids is correct?
options: A) The pyramid of energy can be inverted in the sea because phytoplankton are small
B) In a tree ecosystem the pyramid of number is always upright, because producers are always more numerous
C) Detritus food chains and saprophytes are fully represented in ecological pyramids

D) The pyramid of energy is always upright, because at each step part of the energy is lost as heat (only about 10 % passes on), so energy at a higher level can never exceed that at the lower; the pyramid of biomass in the sea is generally inverted because the small standing crop of fast-multiplying phytoplankton is far less than the biomass of fishes; a single large tree supporting many insects gives an inverted pyramid of number; pyramids do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels, assume a simple food chain, and give no place to saprophytes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Energy pyramid always upright (energy lost at each step); biomass in sea and number for a tree can be inverted; pyramids ignore multiple trophic positions and saprophytes.
Concept: The relationship between producers and consumers in an ecosystem can be graphically represented in the form of a pyramid called an ecological pyramid; the base of each pyramid represents the producers and the apex the top-level consumer. The three ecological pyramids usually studied are of number, biomass and energy. Any calculations of energy content, biomass or numbers have to include all organisms at that trophic level. In most ecosystems all the pyramids are upright; however, there are exceptions: if you count the number of insects feeding on a big tree, the pyramid is inverted, and the pyramid of biomass in the sea is also generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton. The pyramid of energy is always upright and can never be inverted, because when energy flows from a particular trophic level to the next, some energy is always lost as heat at each step; only 10 per cent of the energy is transferred to each trophic level from the lower trophic level. There are certain limitations of ecological pyramids: they do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels; they assume a simple food chain, something that almost never exists in nature, and do not accommodate a food web; moreover, saprophytes are not given any place in ecological pyramids even though they play a vital role in the ecosystem.
Why: Number and biomass are snapshots of standing crop, which can be small where turnover is rapid; energy is a rate of flow, which must decrease at each step by the second law of thermodynamics.
Why not the others: (A) The energy pyramid cannot be inverted. (B) One tree supports many insects, inverting the number pyramid. (C) Saprophytes are given no place.
Key point: Energy pyramid always upright; number and biomass pyramids can be inverted.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting conservation actions as in situ or ex situ, the role of cryopreservation and seed banks, the IUCN Red List, and Ramsar sites
questions.question: A state forest department records four actions: (i) seeds of rare rice varieties stored in a seed bank; (ii) sperm and eggs of an endangered antelope preserved at very low temperature and later used for in vitro fertilisation; (iii) a wetland designated under the Ramsar Convention; (iv) a species added to the IUCN Red List. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) All four are in situ conservation

B) (i) and (ii) are ex situ conservation — taking threatened species out of their natural habitat and protecting them in special settings, gametes being kept viable and fertile for long periods by cryopreservation; (iii) protects a wetland of international importance in its natural setting, i.e. in situ; (iv) is a documentation of the threat status of species, the IUCN Red List (Red Data Book) assessing extinction risk, not a conservation site
C) (iii) is ex situ, since wetlands are man-made; (i) is in situ
D) (iv) means the species is extinct and cannot be conserved
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (i), (ii) ex situ (seed bank, cryopreservation); (iii) in situ (Ramsar wetland); (iv) Red List documentation.
Concept: In in situ (on site) conservation, the endangered species are protected in their natural habitat so that the entire ecosystem is protected; biodiversity hotspots, national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and sacred groves are examples. In ex situ conservation, threatened animals and plants are taken out from their natural habitat and placed in special settings where they can be protected and given special care; zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks serve this purpose. In recent years ex situ conservation has advanced beyond keeping threatened species: gametes of threatened species can now be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods using cryopreservation techniques, eggs can be fertilised in vitro, and plants can be propagated using tissue culture methods; seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods in seed banks. The IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of species and their threat status. The Ramsar Convention protects wetlands of international importance, which are conserved in their natural state.
Step 1: Removal from habitat and protected storage ⇒ ex situ: (i), (ii).
Step 2: Protection of the ecosystem where species live ⇒ in situ: (iii).
Step 3: Assessment and listing of threat status ⇒ (iv), a documentation tool.
Why: The key distinction is whether the organism stays in its natural habitat; listing only measures risk to guide conservation.
Why not the others: (A) Seed banks and cryopreservation are ex situ. (C) Ramsar wetlands are natural habitats. (D) The Red List includes threatened, not only extinct, species.
Key point: In situ = in natural habitat; ex situ = outside it (zoos, seed banks, cryopreservation).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting how many organisms in a list belong to kingdom Protista rather than Monera, using the presence of a nucleus and the major groups of protists
questions.question: Consider: Euglena, Nostoc, Paramecium, a diatom, Plasmodium, Anabaena, Gonyaulax, a slime mould, Mycoplasma. How many of these belong to kingdom Protista?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6 — Euglena, Paramecium, the diatom, Plasmodium, Gonyaulax and the slime mould.
Concept: Kingdom Monera contains the prokaryotes: bacteria, including cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) such as Nostoc and Anabaena, archaebacteria and mycoplasma (organisms that completely lack a cell wall, the smallest living cells known). All single-celled eukaryotes are placed under Protista; being eukaryotes, the protistan cell body contains a well-defined nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles. Protista includes chrysophytes (diatoms and golden algae/desmids), dinoflagellates (e.g. Gonyaulax, which causes red tides), euglenoids (e.g. Euglena), slime moulds (saprophytic protists) and protozoans (amoeboid, flagellated, ciliated such as Paramecium, and sporozoans such as Plasmodium, the malarial parasite).
Given: Nine organisms.
Formula/Principle: Prokaryote (no nucleus) ⇒ Monera; unicellular eukaryote ⇒ Protista.
Step 1: Monera: Nostoc, Anabaena (cyanobacteria), Mycoplasma ⇒ 3.
Step 2: Protista: Euglena (euglenoid), Paramecium (ciliate), diatom (chrysophyte), Plasmodium (sporozoan), Gonyaulax (dinoflagellate), slime mould ⇒ 6.
Step 3: 3 + 6 = 9 ✓.
Why: A nucleus and membrane-bound organelles separate protists from bacteria, even when both are unicellular and photosynthetic.
Why not the others: (A) Counts only protozoa. (B) Includes prokaryotes. (D) Omits some protist groups.
Key point: Cyanobacteria and mycoplasma are Monera; diatoms, dinoflagellates, euglenoids, slime moulds and protozoa are Protista.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Assigning an unknown animal to a non-chordate phylum (Porifera to Aschelminthes) from its excretory structures, body cavity, symmetry and special cells
questions.question: A worm found in the human intestine is bilaterally symmetrical, dorsoventrally flattened, acoelomate, has hooks and suckers, and excretes through flame cells. A second parasite, round in cross-section, has a pseudocoelom and separate sexes. Which identification is correct?
options: A) The first belongs to Platyhelminthes (e.g. Taenia, the tapeworm) and the second to Aschelminthes (e.g. Ascaris); cnidoblasts used for anchorage and capture of prey are typical of Cnidaria, the water canal system with choanocytes of Porifera, and comb plates for locomotion of Ctenophora
B) The first belongs to Cnidaria, because it has suckers; the second to Annelida
C) Both belong to Porifera, because they are parasites
D) The first belongs to Aschelminthes, because it has flame cells; the second to Platyhelminthes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Platyhelminthes (Taenia) and Aschelminthes (Ascaris).
Concept: Phylum Porifera: sponges with a water transport or canal system lined by choanocytes (collar cells). Phylum Cnidaria (Coelenterata): named after the cnidoblasts or cnidocytes (which contain the stinging capsules or nematocysts) present on the tentacles and the body, used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey. Phylum Ctenophora (comb jellies): body bears eight external rows of ciliated comb plates, which help in locomotion; bioluminescence is well marked. Phylum Platyhelminthes (flatworms): dorsoventrally flattened body, bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and acoelomate animals with organ level of organisation; hooks and suckers are present in the parasitic forms; specialised cells called flame cells help in osmoregulation and excretion; e.g. Taenia (tapeworm), Fasciola (liver fluke). Phylum Aschelminthes (roundworms): body circular in cross-section, pseudocoelomate; alimentary canal complete; sexes separate (dioecious); e.g. Ascaris (roundworm), Wuchereria (filarial worm), Ancylostoma (hookworm).
Step 1: Flame cells + dorsoventral flattening + acoelom + hooks/suckers ⇒ Platyhelminthes.
Step 2: Round cross-section + pseudocoelom + separate sexes ⇒ Aschelminthes.
Step 3: The other phyla are identified by their unique cells or structures.
Why: Each phylum has a unique diagnostic feature (choanocytes, cnidoblasts, comb plates, flame cells, pseudocoelom) that identifies it.
Why not the others: (B) Cnidarians are radially symmetrical with cnidoblasts. (C) Porifera are sessile sponges. (D) Flame cells characterise flatworms.
Key point: Flame cells → Platyhelminthes; pseudocoelom → Aschelminthes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the internal structure of dicot and monocot roots and explaining the role of the endodermis with its Casparian strips and of the pericycle
questions.question: Which comparison of dicot and monocot roots, with its explanation, is correct?
options: A) A dicot root usually has two to four xylem bundles, a monocot root more than six (polyarch); both have radial vascular bundles; the endodermis has suberin-impregnated Casparian strips in its radial and tangential walls that are impermeable to water, so water must pass through the cytoplasm of endodermal cells; lateral roots and, in dicots, the vascular cambium during secondary growth arise from the pericycle; monocot roots have a large, well-developed pith and do not undergo secondary growth
B) Monocot roots have two to four xylem bundles and undergo secondary growth
C) Casparian strips are made of cellulose and allow water to pass freely through cell walls
D) Lateral roots arise from the epidermis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Dicot 2–4 xylem bundles, monocot >6; Casparian strips (suberin) force water through cytoplasm; pericycle gives lateral roots and cambium.
Concept: In the dicot root the outermost layer is the epiblema, with root hairs; the cortex consists of several layers of thin-walled parenchyma cells; the innermost layer of the cortex is the endodermis, a single layer of barrel-shaped cells without any intercellular spaces, whose tangential as well as radial walls have a deposition of water-impermeable, waxy material, suberin, in the form of Casparian strips. Next to the endodermis lie a few layers of thick-walled parenchymatous cells referred to as the pericycle; initiation of lateral roots and vascular cambium during secondary growth takes place in these cells. The pith is small or inconspicuous. There are usually two to four xylem and phloem patches. The anatomy of the monocot root is similar to the dicot root in many respects; it has epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, vascular bundles and pith, but as compared to the dicot root which has fewer xylem bundles, there are usually more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles in the monocot root; the pith is large and well developed, and monocotyledonous roots do not undergo any secondary growth.
Why: The suberin band blocks the apoplast route, letting the root control which solutes enter the stele; the pericycle, being meristematic in potential, is the site of new root origin.
Why not the others: (B) Reversed numbers; monocot roots lack secondary growth. (C) Casparian strips are suberin and block water movement through walls. (D) Lateral roots are endogenous, from the pericycle.
Key point: Dicot root 2–4 xylem; monocot polyarch; endodermis with Casparian strips; pericycle → lateral roots.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading the chemical composition of the human erythrocyte membrane and of plant cell walls from a table, and the fluid mosaic model of the membrane
questions.question:
A table summarises cell boundary composition.

Structure | Main components
Human RBC membrane | about 52 % protein, 40 % lipids (mainly phospholipids in a bilayer)
Plant cell wall | cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, proteins
Middle lamella | calcium pectate
Algal cell wall | cellulose, galactans, mannans, minerals such as calcium carbonate

Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The plasma membrane is made almost entirely of cellulose
B) The middle lamella is made of cellulose and lies inside the plasma membrane

C) In the fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972) proteins float in a quasi-fluid lipid bilayer with polar heads facing outwards and hydrophobic tails inwards, allowing lateral movement of proteins; the RBC membrane is in fact richer in protein than in lipid; the middle lamella, mainly calcium pectate, holds neighbouring plant cells together; and plasmodesmata traverse the cell wall and middle lamella to connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells
D) Lipids are arranged as a monolayer with their tails facing outwards
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Fluid mosaic model; RBC membrane ≈52 % protein, 40 % lipid; middle lamella of calcium pectate; plasmodesmata connect cells.
Concept: Detailed structure of the membrane was studied only after the advent of the electron microscope in the 1950s; chemical studies on the cell membrane, especially in human red blood cells (RBCs), enabled scientists to deduce the possible structure of the plasma membrane. These studies showed that the cell membrane is composed of lipids that are arranged in a bilayer, the polar head towards the outer sides and the hydrophobic tails towards the inner part; the membrane also possesses protein and carbohydrate, and the ratio of protein and lipid varies considerably in different cell types — in human beings, the membrane of the erythrocyte has approximately 52 per cent protein and 40 per cent lipids. An improved model of the structure of the cell membrane was proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972), widely accepted as the fluid mosaic model; according to this, the quasi-fluid nature of the lipid enables lateral movement of proteins within the overall bilayer. The algal cell wall is made of cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals like calcium carbonate, while in other plants it consists of cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins; the middle lamella is a layer mainly of calcium pectate which holds or glues the different neighbouring cells together; the cell wall and middle lamellae may be traversed by plasmodesmata which connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.
Given: Composition table.
Step 1: RBC membrane: protein 52 % > lipid 40 % ⇒ protein-rich.
Step 2: Middle lamella = calcium pectate ⇒ intercellular cement.
Step 3: Cellulose is in the wall, outside the membrane.
Why: The amphipathic nature of phospholipids drives bilayer formation, and its fluidity permits protein movement, cell growth, secretion and division.
Why not the others: (A) Cellulose belongs to the wall. (B) The middle lamella is pectate and lies between walls of neighbouring cells. (D) Lipids form a bilayer with tails inwards.
Key point: Fluid mosaic model; RBC membrane 52 % protein; middle lamella = calcium pectate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing primary and secondary metabolites, and the acid-soluble and acid-insoluble fractions of living tissue, including why lipids appear in the acid-insoluble fraction
questions.question: Which comparison about the chemical composition of living tissue is correct?
options: A) Lipids, being of low molecular weight, are found in the acid-soluble fraction
B) Secondary metabolites such as amino acids and sugars have identifiable functions in normal physiological processes
C) Primary metabolites are found only in plants

D) Primary metabolites (amino acids, sugars, nucleotides) have identifiable functions in normal physiology, while secondary metabolites (alkaloids such as morphine and codeine, flavonoids, rubber, essential oils, antibiotics, pigments such as carotenoids) are found mainly in plants, fungi and microbes and many are useful to humans; when tissue is ground in trichloroacetic acid, small molecules (below about 1000 Da) appear in the acid-soluble filtrate, while proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides form the acid-insoluble pellet; lipids, though of molecular weight under 800 Da, also come in the acid-insoluble fraction because on grinding the membranes break into water-insoluble vesicles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Primary vs secondary metabolites; acid-soluble micromolecules vs acid-insoluble macromolecules; lipids in the insoluble fraction because membranes form vesicles.
Concept: To analyse chemical composition, living tissue (vegetable or liver) is ground in trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃CCOOH) using a mortar and pestle to obtain a thick slurry, which on straining gives two fractions: the filtrate (acid-soluble pool) and the retentate (acid-insoluble fraction). Thousands of organic compounds are found in the acid-soluble pool. In animal tissues one notices the presence of all such categories of compounds (amino acids, sugars, nucleotides, lipids) called primary metabolites; when one analyses plant, fungal and microbial cells, one would see thousands of compounds other than these, called secondary metabolites, e.g. alkaloids, flavonoids, rubber, essential oils, antibiotics, coloured pigments, scents, gums and spices. While primary metabolites have identifiable functions and play known roles in normal physiological processes, we do not at the moment understand the role or functions of all the secondary metabolites in host organisms; however, many of them are useful to human welfare (e.g. rubber, drugs, spices, scents and pigments). The acid-soluble pool has chemicals of molecular weights ranging from 18 to around 800 daltons; the acid-insoluble fraction has only four types of organic compounds — proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids — and these classes of compounds, with the exception of lipids, have molecular weights in the range of ten thousand daltons and above. Lipids, whose molecular weights do not exceed 800 Da, come under the acid-insoluble fraction because when we grind a tissue, we are disrupting the cell structure, and cell membranes and other membranes are broken into pieces forming vesicles which are not water soluble.
Why: The fractionation separates by solubility, which normally tracks size, but membrane lipids behave as large aggregates.
Why not the others: (A) Lipids appear in the insoluble fraction. (B) Amino acids and sugars are primary metabolites. (C) Primary metabolites occur in all organisms.
Key point: Acid-insoluble fraction: proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and (as vesicles) lipids.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting how heat, a reducing agent or a change in a single amino acid affects the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure and the function of a protein
questions.question: An enzyme is boiled and loses its activity, though its chain of amino acids is not broken. In a second case, a mutation changes one amino acid in its active site. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) Boiling breaks the peptide bonds, destroying the primary structure

B) Boiling destroys the secondary and tertiary (three-dimensional) structure held by weak bonds, so the active site loses its shape although the primary structure (the sequence of amino acids, held by peptide bonds) remains; the single substitution changes the primary structure itself and may alter folding or the active site; proteins with more than one polypeptide, such as haemoglobin (two α and two β subunits), also have a quaternary structure; the secondary structure includes the right-handed α-helix
C) A change in one amino acid can never affect protein function
D) Haemoglobin has only a tertiary structure, since it is one polypeptide chain
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Heat denatures higher-order structure, leaving the primary structure; a substitution changes the primary structure; haemoglobin has quaternary structure.
Concept: Proteins are polypeptides, linear chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. The structure of proteins is described at four levels. The sequence of amino acids, i.e. the positional information in a protein — which is the first amino acid, which is the second, and so on — is called the primary structure. The protein thread does not exist throughout as an extended rigid rod; the thread is folded in the form of a helix, and only the right-handed helices are observed in proteins; other regions of the protein thread are folded into other forms in what is called the secondary structure. In addition, the long protein chain is also folded upon itself like a hollow woollen ball, giving rise to the tertiary structure; this gives a three-dimensional view of a protein, and tertiary structure is absolutely necessary for the many biological activities of proteins. Some proteins are an assembly of more than one polypeptide or subunit, and the manner in which these individual folded polypeptides or subunits are arranged with respect to each other is the architecture of the protein, otherwise called the quaternary structure; adult human haemoglobin consists of 4 subunits, two of which are identical to each other (α type) and two of which are identical to each other (β type). For enzymes, the active site is a crevice formed by the tertiary folding into which the substrate fits; high temperature destroys enzymatic activity because proteins are denatured by heat.
Why: Enzyme activity depends on the shape of the active site, which is produced by folding stabilised by many weak bonds that heat can break.
Why not the others: (A) Peptide bonds survive boiling. (C) One substitution can alter folding and activity. (D) Haemoglobin has four subunits.
Key point: Primary (sequence) → secondary (helix) → tertiary (3D fold) → quaternary (subunits); heat denatures the higher levels.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Tracking chromosome number and DNA content (C value) through interphase, mitosis and the two meiotic divisions of a cell with 2n = 8
questions.question: A diploid cell has 2n = 8 chromosomes and 2C DNA in G₁. Which statement about chromosome number and DNA content is correct?
options: A) After S phase the cell has 8 chromosomes and 4C DNA; each daughter cell of mitosis has 8 chromosomes and 2C DNA; after meiosis I each cell has 4 chromosomes (each with two chromatids) and 2C DNA, because homologous chromosomes separate; after meiosis II each of the four cells has 4 chromosomes and 1C DNA, because sister chromatids separate; synapsis (zygotene) and crossing over (pachytene) occur only in prophase I
B) After S phase the cell has 16 chromosomes and 4C DNA
C) After meiosis I each cell has 8 chromosomes and 1C DNA, because sister chromatids separate in anaphase I
D) Mitosis halves the chromosome number, and meiosis keeps it constant
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) S: 8 chromosomes, 4C; mitosis: 8, 2C; meiosis I: 4, 2C; meiosis II: 4, 1C.
Concept: During the S or synthesis phase, DNA replication takes place: if the initial amount of DNA is denoted as 2C, it increases to 4C; however, there is no increase in the chromosome number — if the cell had diploid or 2n number of chromosomes at G₁, even after S phase the number of chromosomes remains the same, 2n. Mitosis is an equational division: the chromosome number of the parent is conserved in the daughter cells, the sister chromatids separating at anaphase. Meiosis involves two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division called meiosis I and meiosis II but only a single cycle of DNA replication; meiosis I is initiated after the parental chromosomes have replicated to produce identical sister chromatids at S phase; it involves pairing of homologous chromosomes (synapsis during zygotene) and recombination between non-sister chromatids (crossing over during pachytene); in anaphase I the homologous chromosomes separate, while sister chromatids remain associated at their centromeres; in anaphase II the centromere splits and sister chromatids separate. Four haploid cells are formed at the end of meiosis II.
Step 1: S phase: DNA 2C → 4C; chromosomes stay 8 (now with two chromatids each).
Step 2: Meiosis I separates homologues: 8 → 4 chromosomes, DNA 4C → 2C per cell.
Step 3: Meiosis II separates chromatids: chromosomes stay 4, DNA 2C → 1C per cell.
Why: Chromosome number counts centromeres, which halve only when homologues separate; DNA content halves at each division.
Why not the others: (B) Replication does not double the chromosome number. (C) Sister chromatids stay together in anaphase I. (D) Reversed.
Key point: Meiosis I is reductional (homologues separate); meiosis II is equational (chromatids separate).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting how the levels of RuBP and 3-phosphoglycerate change when light is switched off or CO₂ is lowered, from the use of ATP and NADPH in the Calvin cycle
questions.question: An illuminated green alga is fixing CO₂ steadily. (i) The light is suddenly switched off while CO₂ is kept constant; (ii) in another trial the light is kept on but CO₂ is suddenly lowered. Which prediction about RuBP and PGA (3-phosphoglycerate) levels in the first few seconds is correct?
options: A) (i) RuBP rises and PGA falls; (ii) RuBP falls and PGA rises
B) Neither changes, because the Calvin cycle does not depend on light at all
C) (i) Both rise, because ATP is no longer used

D) (i) PGA rises and RuBP falls, because RuBisCO still carboxylates RuBP into PGA, but the reduction of PGA and the regeneration of RuBP both need ATP (and reduction also NADPH) from the light reactions; (ii) RuBP rises and PGA falls, because RuBP is still regenerated using ATP and NADPH but less is consumed by carboxylation — the Calvin cycle is called a dark reaction only because it does not use light directly, yet it depends on the products of the light reaction
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Light off: PGA ↑, RuBP ↓; CO₂ lowered: RuBP ↑, PGA ↓.
Concept: The products of the light reaction are ATP, NADPH and O₂; of these O₂ diffuses out of the chloroplast while ATP and NADPH are used to drive the processes leading to the synthesis of food, more accurately sugars — this is the biosynthetic phase of photosynthesis. This process does not directly depend on the presence of light but is dependent on the products of the light reaction, i.e. ATP and NADPH, besides CO₂ and H₂O. The Calvin cycle has three stages: carboxylation, the fixation of CO₂ into a stable organic intermediate, catalysed by RuBisCO, in which RuBP combines with CO₂ to form two molecules of 3-PGA; reduction, a series of reactions that lead to the formation of glucose, involving utilisation of 2 molecules of ATP for phosphorylation and two of NADPH for reduction per CO₂ fixed; and regeneration of the CO₂ acceptor RuBP, which requires one ATP for phosphorylation to form RuBP.
Step 1: Light off ⇒ ATP and NADPH run out ⇒ PGA cannot be reduced and RuBP cannot be regenerated.
Step 2: Carboxylation continues briefly on existing RuBP ⇒ PGA accumulates, RuBP is used up.
Step 3: CO₂ lowered ⇒ carboxylation slows, but regeneration continues ⇒ RuBP accumulates, PGA is used up by reduction.
Why: Each intermediate's level depends on the balance between its production and use; switching off one supply shifts the balance predictably.
Why not the others: (A) Reversed predictions. (B) The cycle needs ATP and NADPH from light. (C) RuBP cannot be regenerated without ATP.
Key point: Light off: PGA ↑ RuBP ↓; CO₂ off: RuBP ↑ PGA ↓.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Measuring the respiratory quotient of germinating seeds with a respirometer using KOH to absorb CO₂, and identifying the substrate from the RQ, with the amphibolic nature of respiration
questions.question: Germinating seeds in a respirometer take up 10.0 mL of O₂ in an hour (measured with KOH present to absorb CO₂); without KOH the gas volume shows that 7.0 mL of CO₂ was released in that time. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) RQ = 1.43, so the seeds are respiring carbohydrate

B) RQ = CO₂ released/O₂ consumed = 7.0/10.0 = 0.7, close to the value for fats (e.g. tripalmitin, 102 CO₂ : 145 O₂ ≈ 0.7), so these are probably oil-rich seeds respiring fat; carbohydrates give RQ = 1 and proteins about 0.9; because fatty acids and glycerol enter the respiratory pathway, and intermediates are also withdrawn to make fatty acids and amino acids, respiration is better described as an amphibolic pathway
C) RQ = 0.7 shows anaerobic respiration
D) RQ cannot be measured without knowing the mass of the seeds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) RQ = 0.70 ⇒ fat substrate; respiration is amphibolic.
Concept: The ratio of the volume of CO₂ evolved to the volume of O₂ consumed in respiration is called the respiratory quotient (RQ): RQ = volume of CO₂ evolved / volume of O₂ consumed. The respiratory quotient depends upon the type of respiratory substrate used during respiration. When carbohydrates are used as substrate and are completely oxidised, the RQ will be 1, because equal amounts of CO₂ and O₂ are evolved and consumed. When fats are used in respiration the RQ is less than 1; e.g. for tripalmitin, 2(C₅₁H₉₈O₆) + 145 O₂ → 102 CO₂ + 98 H₂O + energy, RQ = 102/145 = 0.7. When proteins are respiratory substrates the ratio would be about 0.9. Fats would need to be broken down into glycerol and fatty acids first; if fatty acids were to be respired they would first be degraded to acetyl CoA and enter the pathway, while glycerol would enter after being converted to PGAL; proteins are degraded by proteases, and the individual amino acids, after deamination, enter the pathway at some stage within the Krebs cycle or even as pyruvate or acetyl CoA. Because the respiratory pathway is involved in both anabolism and catabolism, it would hence be better to consider it an amphibolic pathway rather than a catabolic one.
Given: O₂ consumed = 10.0 mL; CO₂ released = 7.0 mL.
Formula/Principle: RQ = V(CO₂)/V(O₂).
Step 1: RQ = 7.0/10.0 = 0.70.
Step 2: Compare: carbohydrate 1.0; protein ≈ 0.9; fat ≈ 0.7.
Step 3: 0.70 ⇒ fat ⇒ oil-rich seeds.
Why: Fats are poorer in oxygen than carbohydrates, so more external O₂ is needed per CO₂ released, lowering the RQ.
Why not the others: (A) Ratio inverted. (C) Anaerobic respiration releases CO₂ without consuming O₂, giving RQ > 1 (or infinite). (D) RQ is a ratio of volumes, independent of mass.
Key point: RQ: carbohydrate 1, protein ≈ 0.9, fat ≈ 0.7.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the effects of drugs that block or mimic the sympathetic or parasympathetic system on heart rate, pupil size and digestion, within the organisation of the peripheral nervous system
questions.question: In an animal experiment, drug X blocks the action of the parasympathetic nerves on the organs, while drug Y mimics the effect of sympathetic stimulation. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) X slows the heart and constricts the pupil; Y increases digestive activity
B) X and Y both act on skeletal muscles, since they belong to the somatic nervous system

C) Both drugs tend to increase heart rate and dilate the pupil, since the autonomic nervous system — the part of the peripheral nervous system relaying impulses from the CNS to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles — has two divisions with generally opposite effects: removing parasympathetic action leaves sympathetic effects unopposed; the somatic neural system instead relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles, and the visceral nervous system is the part of the PNS comprising the network of nerves, fibres and ganglia that carries impulses between the CNS and the viscera
D) Both drugs slow the heart, because the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems have the same effects
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Both raise heart rate and dilate the pupil; sympathetic and parasympathetic act oppositely; somatic system serves skeletal muscle.
Concept: The neural system of human beings is divided into two parts: the central neural system (CNS) and the peripheral neural system (PNS); the PNS comprises all the nerves of the body associated with the CNS (brain and spinal cord). The nerve fibres of the PNS are of two types: afferent fibres, which transmit impulses from tissues/organs to the CNS, and efferent fibres, which transmit regulatory impulses from the CNS to the concerned peripheral tissues/organs. The PNS is divided into two divisions, the somatic neural system and the autonomic neural system; the somatic neural system relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles, while the autonomic neural system transmits impulses from the CNS to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles of the body; the autonomic neural system is further classified into the sympathetic neural system and the parasympathetic neural system. The visceral nervous system is the part of the peripheral nervous system that comprises the whole complex of nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses by which impulses travel from the CNS to the viscera and from the viscera to the CNS. The sympathetic system prepares the body for emergencies (raised heart rate, dilated pupils, reduced digestion), while the parasympathetic system restores rest conditions.
Given: X blocks parasympathetic action; Y mimics sympathetic action.
Step 1: Parasympathetic normally slows the heart and constricts the pupil; blocking it ⇒ faster heart, dilated pupil.
Step 2: Sympathetic stimulation itself ⇒ faster heart, dilated pupil, reduced digestion.
Step 3: Hence both drugs give similar effects on these organs.
Why: Organs with dual autonomic supply are set by the balance of two opposing inputs, so removing one is like strengthening the other.
Why not the others: (A) Effects reversed. (B) These drugs act on the autonomic system controlling involuntary organs. (D) The two divisions oppose each other.
Key point: Sympathetic and parasympathetic oppose each other; blocking one mimics the other.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Writing electronic configurations by the Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule, including the exceptional configurations of Cr and Cu and unpaired electrons in ions
questions.question: Which statement about electronic configurations, with its reason, is correct?
options: A) Cr is [Ar]3d⁴4s² and Cu is [Ar]3d⁹4s², exactly as the Aufbau order predicts
B) An orbital can hold three electrons if one of them has a different value of n
C) In nitrogen the three 2p electrons pair up in one orbital first, because pairing lowers the energy

D) Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹, because exactly half-filled and completely filled subshells are extra stable (symmetry and larger exchange energy); by the Pauli principle no two electrons in an atom have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin; by Hund's rule nitrogen's three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins (3 unpaired); Fe³⁺ ([Ar]3d⁵) has 5 unpaired electrons, since the 4s electrons are lost first
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cr 3d⁵4s¹, Cu 3d¹⁰4s¹ (stable half-filled/filled subshells); Pauli: ≤ 2 electrons per orbital; Hund: N has 3 unpaired; Fe³⁺ has 5 unpaired.
Concept: The Aufbau principle states that in the ground state of atoms, the orbitals are filled in order of their increasing energies. The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers; only two electrons may exist in the same orbital and these electrons must have opposite spin. Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity states that pairing of electrons in the orbitals belonging to the same subshell (p, d or f) does not take place until each orbital belonging to that subshell has got one electron each, i.e. is singly occupied. Fully filled and half-filled orbitals have extra stability; e.g. the valence electronic configurations of Cr and Cu are 3d⁵4s¹ and 3d¹⁰4s¹ respectively and not 3d⁴4s² and 3d⁹4s²; the stability arises from symmetry and from exchange energy, which is maximum when the subshell is either half-filled or completely filled. When transition metals form cations, the 4s electrons are removed before the 3d electrons.
Given: Z: N 7, Cr 24, Fe 26, Cu 29.
Step 1: Cr: 3d⁴4s² → 3d⁵4s¹ gives a half-filled 3d subshell plus half-filled 4s.
Step 2: Cu: 3d⁹4s² → 3d¹⁰4s¹ gives a completely filled 3d subshell.
Step 3: Fe [Ar]3d⁶4s² → Fe³⁺ [Ar]3d⁵ ⇒ five singly occupied d orbitals ⇒ 5 unpaired.
Why: Electrons with parallel spins in degenerate orbitals can exchange positions, releasing exchange energy; the maximum number of such exchanges occurs in half-filled and filled subshells.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores the extra stability of d⁵ and d¹⁰. (B) Pauli limits each orbital to two electrons. (C) Hund's rule says the reverse.
Key point: Aufbau + Pauli + Hund; d⁵ and d¹⁰ extra stable; cations lose 4s first.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the anomalous behaviour of the first element of groups 1, 2 and 13 (Li, Be, B) and their diagonal similarities, in terms of small size, high charge density and absence of d orbitals
questions.question: Which statement about the first members of groups 1, 2 and 13 is correct, with the right reason?
options: A) Lithium behaves exactly like the other alkali metals, forming a peroxide in excess air

B) Lithium differs from other alkali metals and resembles magnesium (diagonal relationship) because of its very small size and high polarising power: it forms the monoxide Li₂O and the nitride Li₃N directly, and LiCl is deliquescent and more covalent; beryllium resembles aluminium, BeCl₂ being covalent and its oxide amphoteric; the maximum covalency of Be is 4 and of B is 4, because the second period has no d orbitals, so boron cannot form [BF₆]³⁻ while aluminium forms [AlF₆]³⁻
C) Boron forms [BF₆]³⁻ readily, because it is in the same group as aluminium
D) Beryllium oxide is strongly basic like barium oxide
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Li resembles Mg, Be resembles Al (small size, high polarising power); Li₂O, Li₃N; maximum covalency 4 for Be and B (no d orbitals).
Concept: The first member of each of the groups 1 (lithium) and 2 (beryllium) and groups 13–17 (boron to fluorine) differs in many respects from the other members of their respective group; the anomalous behaviour is attributed to their small size, large charge/radius ratio and high electronegativity. In addition, the first member of a group has only four valence orbitals (2s and 2p) available for bonding, whereas the second member of the group has nine valence orbitals (3s, 3p, 3d); as a consequence, the maximum covalency of the first member of each group is 4 (e.g. boron can only form [BF₄]⁻), whereas the other members can expand their valence shell to accommodate more than four pairs of electrons (e.g. aluminium forms [AlF₆]³⁻). Lithium, unlike other alkali metals, forms only the monoxide Li₂O when burnt in air and combines directly with nitrogen to form the nitride Li₃N, as does magnesium; LiCl is deliquescent and crystallises as a hydrate LiCl·2H₂O. The anomalous behaviour of beryllium is due to its exceptionally small atomic and ionic size and high ionisation enthalpy; beryllium forms covalent compounds, its oxide and hydroxide are amphoteric, and it shows a diagonal relationship to aluminium.
Why: A small, highly charged cation distorts neighbouring anions strongly, giving covalent character and similarities with the diagonally placed element of similar charge/radius ratio.
Why not the others: (A) Li forms the monoxide, not a peroxide. (C) B lacks d orbitals; its maximum covalency is 4. (D) BeO is amphoteric.
Key point: First members: small size, high polarising power, no d orbitals ⇒ anomalies and diagonal relationships.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the dipole moment of water from O–H bond moments and bond angle, explaining zero dipoles of symmetric molecules, and ordering covalent character with Fajans' rules
questions.question: Each O–H bond moment is 1.5 D and the H–O–H angle is 104.5° (cos 52.25° = 0.612). Which statement is correct?
options: A) μ(H₂O) = 3.0 D, the sum of the two bond moments; CO₂ has a dipole because each C=O bond is polar
B) μ(H₂O) = 0, because the bond moments cancel; LiF is more covalent than LiI

C) μ(H₂O) = 2 × 1.5 × cos 52.25° ≈ 1.84 D, the vector sum of the two bond moments; linear CO₂ and planar BF₃ have zero dipole moment because their bond moments cancel; by Fajans' rules covalent character increases with the polarising power of the cation and the polarisability of the anion, so LiI > LiCl > LiF and AlCl₃ > MgCl₂ > NaCl in covalent character
D) μ(H₂O) = 1.5 D; covalent character is independent of ion size
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) μ ≈ 1.84 D; CO₂, BF₃ zero; covalent character LiI > LiCl > LiF, AlCl₃ > MgCl₂ > NaCl.
Concept: Dipole moment is defined as the product of the magnitude of the charge and the distance between the centres of positive and negative charge; it is a vector quantity. In the case of polyatomic molecules the dipole moment depends not only upon the individual dipole moments of bonds (bond dipoles) but also on the spatial arrangement of the various bonds in the molecule; in such cases the dipole moment of a molecule is the vector sum of the dipole moments of the various bonds. CO₂ is linear and BF₃ is trigonal planar, so their bond dipoles cancel, giving zero net dipole moment. Just as all covalent bonds have some partial ionic character, ionic bonds also have partial covalent character, discussed by Fajans in terms of the following rules: the smaller the size of the cation and the larger the size of the anion, the greater the covalent character of an ionic bond; the greater the charge on the cation, the greater the covalent character of the ionic bond.
Given: μ(O–H) = 1.5 D; ∠HOH = 104.5°.
Formula/Principle: Resultant of two equal vectors at angle θ: μ = 2μ₁ cos(θ/2).
Step 1: θ/2 = 52.25°; cos 52.25° = 0.612.
Step 2: μ = 2 × 1.5 × 0.612 = 1.84 D.
Step 3: Fajans: Li⁺ small; I⁻ most polarisable ⇒ LiI most covalent; charge Al³⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Na⁺ ⇒ AlCl₃ most covalent.
Why: Bond dipoles add as vectors, so geometry decides whether they reinforce or cancel; a small, highly charged cation distorts the electron cloud of a large anion towards itself.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores the angle; CO₂ dipoles cancel. (B) Bent H₂O does not cancel; LiI is more covalent. (D) Wrong value; size matters.
Key point: μ = vector sum of bond moments; Fajans: small, highly charged cation + large anion ⇒ covalent character.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Using Hess's law to obtain enthalpies of reactions that cannot be measured directly — the formation of CO and the graphite-to-diamond transition — from combustion enthalpies
questions.question: Given C(graphite) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹; CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283.0 kJ mol⁻¹; C(diamond) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −395.4 kJ mol⁻¹. Which result is correct?
options: A) ΔfH(CO) = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹, obtained as −393.5 − (−283.0), since enthalpy is a state function and the path C → CO → CO₂ must give the same total as C → CO₂ directly; and C(graphite) → C(diamond) has ΔH = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹, so graphite is the more stable form and the standard state of carbon
B) ΔfH(CO) = −676.5 kJ mol⁻¹, the sum of the two combustion enthalpies
C) ΔfH(CO) = +110.5 kJ mol⁻¹; graphite → diamond is −1.9 kJ mol⁻¹
D) Hess's law cannot be used because CO formation cannot be carried out cleanly
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ΔfH(CO) = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹; graphite → diamond = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
Concept: Hess's law of constant heat summation: if a reaction takes place in several steps, its standard reaction enthalpy is the sum of the standard enthalpies of the intermediate reactions into which the overall reaction may be divided at the same temperature. Enthalpy is a state function, hence the change in enthalpy is independent of the path between the initial state (reactants) and the final state (products). It is difficult to burn carbon to CO only, as some CO₂ always forms, so ΔfH(CO) is found indirectly from combustion data. The standard state of carbon is graphite, the most stable form at 1 bar and 298 K.
Given: ΔcH(graphite) = −393.5; ΔcH(CO) = −283.0; ΔcH(diamond) = −395.4 kJ mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: Path 1 (C → CO₂) = Path 2 (C → CO → CO₂).
Step 1: −393.5 = ΔfH(CO) + (−283.0).
Step 2: ΔfH(CO) = −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 3: Graphite → diamond: (−393.5) − (−395.4) = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
Worked derivation: C(gr) + O₂ → CO₂ (−393.5); CO₂ → C(dia) + O₂ (+395.4); sum: C(gr) → C(dia), +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why: Reversing an equation reverses the sign of ΔH; adding equations adds their ΔH, so unmeasurable reactions follow from measurable ones.
Why not the others: (B) The second equation must be reversed, not added. (C) Signs reversed. (D) Hess's law is used exactly for such indirect determinations.
Key point: ΔH is path-independent; reverse an equation ⇒ change sign.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Predicting pH meter readings for a strong acid partly neutralised by a strong base, a diluted strong acid and a dilute strong base
questions.question: A student records pH meter readings at 298 K for: (i) 25.0 mL of 0.20 M HCl mixed with 25.0 mL of 0.10 M NaOH; (ii) an HCl solution of pH 2.0 diluted 100 times with water; (iii) 0.0010 M NaOH. Which set of readings is expected?
options: A) (i) 1.30; (ii) 4.0; (iii) 11.0 — in (i), 2.5 mmol of HCl remain in 50 mL, so [H⁺] = 0.050 M; in (ii) [H⁺] falls from 10⁻² to 10⁻⁴ M; in (iii) pOH = 3
B) (i) 7.0, because acid and base were mixed; (ii) 2.0; (iii) 3.0
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) pH 1.30, 4.0, 11.0.
Concept: For strong acids and bases, which dissociate completely, pH = −log[H⁺] and pOH = −log[OH⁻], with pH + pOH = 14 at 298 K. When a strong acid is mixed with a strong base, H⁺ and OH⁻ neutralise each other mole for mole, and the pH is decided by whichever is in excess, divided by the total volume. Dilution by a factor of 10 changes [H⁺] by a factor of 10 and pH by one unit, as long as the acid concentration remains well above 10⁻⁷ M.
Given: (i) n(H⁺) = 25.0 × 0.20 = 5.0 mmol; n(OH⁻) = 25.0 × 0.10 = 2.5 mmol; total volume 50.0 mL.
Formula/Principle: pH = −log[H⁺]; pOH = −log[OH⁻]; pH + pOH = 14.
Step 1: Excess H⁺ = 2.5 mmol in 50.0 mL ⇒ [H⁺] = 0.050 M ⇒ pH = 1.30.
Step 2: pH 2.0 ⇒ [H⁺] = 10⁻² M; diluted 100× ⇒ 10⁻⁴ M ⇒ pH 4.0.
Step 3: [OH⁻] = 10⁻³ M ⇒ pOH = 3 ⇒ pH = 11.0.
Why: The excess reagent determines pH after neutralisation, and total volume must be used for concentration.
Why not the others: (B) The acid is in excess, so pH < 7; dilution changes pH; NaOH gives pH > 7. (C) Uses the original volume and confuses dilution with multiplication. (D) Wrong excess concentration and pOH.
Key point: After mixing, use the excess moles over the total volume; ×100 dilution of a strong acid ⇒ pH + 2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading successive ionisation constants of phosphoric acid and explaining why they fall steeply, which equilibrium sets the pH, and trends in acid strength
questions.question: For H₃PO₄ at 298 K: Ka₁ = 7.5 × 10⁻³, Ka₂ = 6.2 × 10⁻⁸, Ka₃ = 4.2 × 10⁻¹³. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) All three protons are released equally, so [H⁺] = 3 × the acid concentration
B) Ka₃ is the largest, because the third proton is the easiest to remove
C) H₃PO₄ is a strong acid, as strong as HCl

D) Each successive Ka is much smaller because it is harder to remove a positively charged proton from an increasingly negatively charged ion (H₂PO₄⁻, then HPO₄²⁻); hence the [H⁺] of the solution comes almost entirely from the first ionisation, and in a solution of the acid [HPO₄²⁻] is approximately equal to Ka₂; for binary acids of a group, acid strength increases HF < HCl < HBr < HI as the H–X bond becomes weaker, though electronegativity falls
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ka₁ ≫ Ka₂ ≫ Ka₃ (charge effect); first step sets [H⁺]; [HPO₄²⁻] ≈ Ka₂; HF < HCl < HBr < HI.
Concept: A polybasic or polyprotic acid has more than one ionisable proton per molecule; e.g. phosphoric acid ionises in three steps, with constants Ka₁, Ka₂, Ka₃. It is observed that higher order ionisation constants are smaller than the lower order ionisation constants, Ka₁ > Ka₂ > Ka₃; the reason is that it is more difficult to remove a positively charged proton from a negative ion due to electrostatic forces. Since Ka₁ is much larger than the others, the H⁺ concentration of a polyprotic acid solution is determined mainly by the first ionisation. The strength of an acid H–A depends on the strength and polarity of the H–A bond; down a group, the H–A bond strength is a more important factor than polarity, and as the bond strength decreases the acid strength increases, so HF < HCl < HBr < HI.
Given: Ka₁ : Ka₂ : Ka₃ ≈ 10⁻² : 10⁻⁷ : 10⁻¹².
Step 1: Ka₁/Ka₂ ≈ 10⁵ ⇒ second ionisation negligible compared with the first in setting [H⁺].
Step 2: In Ka₂ = [H⁺][HPO₄²⁻]/[H₂PO₄⁻], [H⁺] ≈ [H₂PO₄⁻] from step 1 ⇒ [HPO₄²⁻] ≈ Ka₂.
Step 3: Third ionisation is weaker still (Ka₃ ≈ 10⁻¹³).
Why: Each proton removed leaves a more negative ion that holds the next proton more strongly.
Why not the others: (A) Later protons are barely released. (B) Ka₃ is the smallest. (C) Ka₁ = 7.5 × 10⁻³ is far below a strong acid.
Key point: Ka₁ ≫ Ka₂ ≫ Ka₃; [H⁺] from the first step; binary acid strength rises as H–X bond weakens.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Finding average and actual oxidation numbers of atoms in compounds where identical atoms are in different environments, using their structures (Br₃O₈, C₃O₂, Fe₃O₄, NH₄NO₃)
questions.question: Which statement about oxidation numbers is correct?
options: A) In Br₃O₈ every bromine atom has oxidation number exactly 16/3; fractional oxidation numbers are actual values for each atom

B) In Br₃O₈ the average oxidation number of Br is +16/3, but from the structure the two terminal Br atoms are +6 and the central Br is +4; in C₃O₂ (O=C=C=C=O) the average is +4/3, the end carbons being +2 and the central carbon 0; in Fe₃O₄ the average is +8/3, corresponding to one Fe²⁺ and two Fe³⁺; in NH₄NO₃ the two nitrogens are −3 and +5, not both +1
C) In NH₄NO₃ both nitrogen atoms are +1, the average value
D) In Fe₃O₄ all iron atoms are +3
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Br₃O₈: average +16/3 (actual +6, +4, +6); C₃O₂: +4/3 (+2, 0, +2); Fe₃O₄: +8/3 (Fe²⁺ + 2Fe³⁺); NH₄NO₃: −3 and +5.
Concept: Oxidation number denotes the oxidation state of an element in a compound ascertained according to a set of rules formulated on the basis that the electron pair in a chemical bond belongs to the more electronegative element. The oxidation number calculated from the formula is the average when the same element is present in different bonding environments. Sometimes we come across certain elements in compounds in fractional oxidation states, e.g. C₃O₂ (where the oxidation number of carbon is 4/3), Br₃O₈ (16/3) and Na₂S₄O₆ (2.5); the idea of a fractional oxidation state should be taken with care, as the structure reveals that the element is present in different oxidation states: in the structure of Br₃O₈, each of the two terminal bromine atoms is present in the oxidation state of +6 and the middle bromine is present in the +4 oxidation state; once again the average of these, 16/3, is fractional. Similarly, the structure of C₃O₂ shows the end carbons at +2 and the middle carbon at 0.
Given: Br₃O₈, C₃O₂, Fe₃O₄, NH₄NO₃; O = −2, H = +1.
Step 1: Br₃O₈: 3x + 8(−2) = 0 ⇒ x = 16/3; structure: (6 + 4 + 6)/3 = 16/3 ✓.
Step 2: C₃O₂: 3x − 4 = 0 ⇒ 4/3; (2 + 0 + 2)/3 = 4/3 ✓; Fe₃O₄: 3x − 8 = 0 ⇒ 8/3 = (2 + 3 + 3)/3 ✓.
Step 3: NH₄⁺: x + 4 = +1 ⇒ −3; NO₃⁻: x − 6 = −1 ⇒ +5.
Why: Oxidation numbers are assigned atom by atom from bonding; the formula only gives their average.
Why not the others: (A) A fractional value is only an average. (C) The two nitrogen atoms are in different ions. (D) Iron is in two states in Fe₃O₄.
Key point: Fractional oxidation number = average of different actual states revealed by structure.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Choosing purification methods for organic compounds — sublimation, fractional distillation, distillation under reduced pressure, differential extraction and chromatography — and calculating an Rf value
questions.question: Which choice of method and reason is correct?
options: A) Naphthalene mixed with common salt is separated by fractional distillation; Rf = distance moved by solvent ÷ distance moved by the substance
B) Two miscible liquids boiling at 353 K and 356 K are separated by simple distillation; chromatography works only for coloured compounds

C) Naphthalene is separated from common salt by sublimation, since naphthalene passes directly from solid to vapour; two miscible liquids with close boiling points (e.g. 353 K and 383 K, or closer) need fractional distillation, where repeated vaporisation and condensation in the fractionating column enrich the vapour in the more volatile liquid; a liquid that decomposes below its normal boiling point is distilled under reduced pressure; an organic compound is extracted from water into an immiscible solvent in which it is more soluble (differential extraction); in a TLC run, a spot that moves 2.4 cm while the solvent front moves 6.0 cm has Rf = 2.4/6.0 = 0.40
