D) Distillation under reduced pressure is used for liquids that are stable well above their boiling points
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Sublimation; fractional distillation; reduced-pressure distillation; differential extraction; Rf = 0.40.
Concept: Sublimation: some solid substances change from solid to vapour state without passing through the liquid state; the purification technique based on this principle is known as sublimation and is used to separate sublimable compounds from non-sublimable impurities. Distillation: this important method is used to separate (i) volatile liquids from non-volatile impurities and (ii) liquids having sufficient difference in their boiling points. Fractional distillation: if the difference in boiling points of two liquids is not much, simple distillation cannot be used to separate them; the vapours of a liquid mixture are passed through a fractionating column, which provides many surfaces for heat exchange between the ascending vapours and the descending condensed liquid, so the vapours become richer in the more volatile component. Distillation under reduced pressure is used to purify liquids having very high boiling points and those which decompose at or below their boiling points; such liquids are made to boil at a temperature lower than their normal boiling points by reducing the pressure on their surface. Differential extraction: when an organic compound is present in an aqueous medium, it is separated by shaking it with an organic solvent in which it is more soluble than in water; the organic solvent and the aqueous solution should be immiscible with each other. In thin layer chromatography, the relative adsorption of each component of the mixture is expressed in terms of its retardation factor, Rf = distance moved by the substance from the base line ÷ distance moved by the solvent from the base line; colourless compounds can be detected under UV light or by iodine or spraying reagents.
Given: Spot distance 2.4 cm; solvent front 6.0 cm.
Step 1: Rf = 2.4/6.0 = 0.40.
Why: Each method exploits a physical difference between the compound and the impurity — volatility, solubility or adsorption.
Why not the others: (A) Sublimation, not distillation, and the Rf ratio is inverted. (B) Close boiling points need fractional distillation; colourless spots can be detected. (D) Reduced pressure is for liquids that decompose at or below their boiling points.
Key point: Match the method to the property difference; Rf = substance distance ÷ solvent distance.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Evidence that benzene is not a simple cyclohexatriene — equal bond lengths, one ortho-disubstituted product, resistance to addition — and its explanation by resonance and aromaticity
questions.question: Which statement about the structure of benzene is correct?
options: A) Benzene has three C–C bonds of 154 pm and three C=C bonds of 134 pm, as in the Kekulé structure
B) Benzene readily decolourises bromine water by addition, like ethene

C) All six C–C bonds in benzene are 139 pm, between single (154 pm) and double (134 pm) bond lengths; only one ortho-disubstituted product forms, not the two that a fixed Kekulé structure predicts; benzene prefers substitution to addition because the six π electrons are delocalised over the ring (resonance hybrid of two Kekulé structures), giving extra stability; it is aromatic since it is planar, cyclic and has (4n + 2) π electrons with n = 1
D) Benzene is unstable because it has three double bonds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Equal 139 pm bonds; one ortho product; delocalised 6π electrons give stability and substitution; Hückel 4n + 2.
Concept: Kekulé in 1865 proposed a cyclic arrangement of six carbon atoms with alternate single and double bonds; but the Kekulé structure failed to explain why benzene shows only one ortho-disubstituted product, whereas his structure would predict two isomeric 1,2-dibromobenzenes. To overcome this, Kekulé suggested oscillating double bonds; benzene is now represented as a hybrid of various resonating structures. The X-ray diffraction data reveal that benzene is a planar molecule, and that all six C–C bond lengths are of the same order (139 pm), intermediate between C–C single bond (154 pm) and C=C double bond (133–134 pm); thus the absence of pure double bonds in benzene accounts for the reluctance of benzene to show addition reactions under normal conditions, explaining the unusual behaviour of benzene. The orbital overlap gives us a better picture of the structure: the unhybridised p orbitals of the six sp² carbons overlap sideways to form a π electron cloud above and below the ring, and the delocalisation of π electrons results in stability. Aromatic compounds follow Hückel's rule: planarity, complete delocalisation of the π electrons in the ring, and presence of (4n + 2) π electrons in the ring, where n is an integer (n = 0, 1, 2, ...).
Why: Delocalisation lowers the energy of the ring; addition would destroy this, so benzene reacts by substitution, which keeps the aromatic sextet.
Why not the others: (A) X-ray data show equal bonds. (B) Benzene does not undergo addition under normal conditions. (D) Benzene is unusually stable.
Key point: Benzene: equal 139 pm bonds, resonance-stabilised, aromatic (6π), substitution not addition.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the osmotic pressure of physiological saline, the isotonic concentration of glucose, and what happens to red blood cells in hypotonic and hypertonic solutions and in reverse osmosis
questions.question: "Normal saline" is 0.90 % (w/v) NaCl (M = 58.5), assumed completely dissociated. Which statement is correct at 310 K (R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)?
options: A) π = 3.9 atm, since NaCl does not dissociate; a 0.90 % glucose solution is isotonic with it
B) π = 0.78 atm; red blood cells shrink in pure water
C) π = 15.6 atm; glucose of 0.154 M is isotonic

D) π = iCRT = 2 × 0.154 × 0.0821 × 310 ≈ 7.8 atm; a glucose solution isotonic with it needs 0.308 M (about 5.5 % w/v); red blood cells swell and may burst in water (hypotonic) and shrink in concentrated salt solution (hypertonic); applying a pressure larger than π to the solution side drives water out of it through a semipermeable membrane (reverse osmosis, used for desalination)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) π ≈ 7.8 atm; isotonic glucose 0.308 M (≈ 5.5 %); hypotonic → swelling, hypertonic → shrinking; reverse osmosis.
Concept: The osmotic pressure of a dilute solution is proportional to its molarity at a given temperature: π = CRT, and for electrolytes π = iCRT, where i is the van't Hoff factor (≈ 2 for NaCl). Two solutions having the same osmotic pressure at a given temperature are called isotonic solutions; when such solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane no osmosis occurs between them. The osmotic pressure associated with the fluid inside the blood cell is equivalent to that of 0.9 % (mass/volume) sodium chloride solution, called normal saline, and it is safe to inject intravenously. If we place the cells in a solution containing more than 0.9 % NaCl, water will flow out of the cells and they will shrink (hypertonic); if the salt concentration is less than 0.9 %, water will flow into the cells and they will swell (hypotonic). The direction of osmosis can be reversed if a pressure larger than the osmotic pressure is applied to the solution side; pure solvent then flows out of the solution through the semipermeable membrane — reverse osmosis, used in desalination of sea water.
Given: 0.90 g NaCl per 100 mL ⇒ 9.0 g L⁻¹; M = 58.5; i = 2; T = 310 K.
Formula/Principle: π = iCRT.
Step 1: C = 9.0/58.5 = 0.154 mol L⁻¹.
Step 2: π = 2 × 0.154 × 0.0821 × 310 = 7.83 atm.
Step 3: Isotonic glucose (i = 1): C = 0.308 M ⇒ 0.308 × 180 = 55.4 g L⁻¹ ≈ 5.5 %.
Why: Osmotic pressure counts dissolved particles; NaCl gives two per formula unit, so a non-electrolyte must be twice as concentrated to match.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores dissociation; 0.9 % glucose is hypotonic. (B) Calculation wrong; cells swell in water. (C) Doubles twice; 0.154 M glucose is hypotonic.
Key point: π = iCRT; isotonic = equal particle concentration; RBCs swell in hypotonic, shrink in hypertonic solution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Applying the Nernst equation to a Ni–Ag cell with non-standard concentrations, and linking its emf to ΔG and to the equilibrium constant
questions.question: For the cell Ni(s) | Ni²⁺(0.10 M) || Ag⁺(0.0010 M) | Ag(s) at 298 K, E°(Ni²⁺/Ni) = −0.25 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V. Which set of results is correct (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)?
options: A) E°cell = 1.05 V; Ecell = 1.05 − (0.0591/2) log[0.10/(0.0010)²] = 1.05 − 0.148 ≈ 0.90 V; ΔG = −nFE = −2 × 96 500 × 0.90 ≈ −174 kJ mol⁻¹; log K = 2 × 1.05/0.0591 ≈ 35.5, so the reaction goes practically to completion
B) Ecell = 1.05 V, since concentrations do not affect emf; ΔG = +203 kJ mol⁻¹
C) Ecell = 1.20 V; log K = 17.8, because n = 1
D) Ecell = 0.55 V, since E° = 0.80 − 0.25; ΔG = −106 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) E ≈ 0.90 V; ΔG ≈ −174 kJ mol⁻¹; log K ≈ 35.5.
Concept: For the general electrochemical reaction, the Nernst equation gives Ecell = E°cell − (2.303RT/nF) log Q, which at 298 K becomes Ecell = E°cell − (0.0591/n) log Q, where Q has the same form as the equilibrium constant but uses the actual concentrations; pure solids have activity 1. Electrical work done in one second equals the electrical potential multiplied by the total charge passed; ΔrG = −nFEcell, and if the cell emf is positive, ΔrG is negative and the reaction is spontaneous. At equilibrium Ecell = 0, so E°cell = (0.0591/n) log Kc at 298 K.
Given: Ni + 2Ag⁺ → Ni²⁺ + 2Ag; n = 2; [Ni²⁺] = 0.10 M; [Ag⁺] = 0.0010 M.
Formula/Principle: E = E° − (0.0591/n) log([Ni²⁺]/[Ag⁺]²); ΔG = −nFE; log K = nE°/0.0591.
Step 1: E° = 0.80 − (−0.25) = 1.05 V.
Step 2: Q = 0.10/(10⁻³)² = 10⁵; E = 1.05 − 0.02955 × 5 = 0.902 V.
Step 3: ΔG = −2 × 96 500 × 0.902 = −1.74 × 10⁵ J = −174 kJ mol⁻¹; log K = 2.10/0.0591 = 35.5.
Why: A low concentration of the cathode ion (Ag⁺) and a high concentration of the product ion (Ni²⁺) make Q large and reduce the driving force below the standard value.
Why not the others: (B) Concentrations do affect emf; ΔG is negative. (C) n = 2, and the emf must fall when Q > 1. (D) E° is a difference of reduction potentials: 0.80 − (−0.25).
Key point: E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q; ΔG = −nFE; log K = nE°/0.0591.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Determining the order of a reaction from how its half-life depends on initial concentration, and calculating the rate constant for a second-order reaction
questions.question: For A → products, the half-life is 25 s when [A]₀ = 0.40 M, 50 s when [A]₀ = 0.20 M and 100 s when [A]₀ = 0.10 M. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) First order, because the half-life is measured; k = 0.0277 s⁻¹

B) Second order, because t½ is inversely proportional to [A]₀ (t½ = 1/(k[A]₀)); k = 1/(25 × 0.40) = 0.10 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; for a zero-order reaction t½ = [A]₀/2k would instead be directly proportional to [A]₀, and for a first-order reaction t½ = 0.693/k would be constant
C) Zero order, because t½ changes with concentration; k = 0.008 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
D) Order cannot be found from half-lives
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Second order; k = 0.10 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Concept: The half-life of a reaction is the time in which the concentration of a reactant is reduced to one half of its initial concentration. For a zero order reaction t½ = [R]₀/2k, so t½ is directly proportional to the initial concentration; for a first order reaction t½ = 0.693/k, independent of [R]₀; for a second-order reaction 1/[R] − 1/[R]₀ = kt, giving t½ = 1/(k[R]₀), inversely proportional to [R]₀. In general t½ ∝ [R]₀^(1−n) for an nth-order reaction, which allows the order to be read from the trend.
Given: [A]₀ = 0.40, 0.20, 0.10 M; t½ = 25, 50, 100 s.
Formula/Principle: t½ ∝ [A]₀^(1−n).
Step 1: Halving [A]₀ doubles t½ ⇒ t½ ∝ [A]₀⁻¹ ⇒ 1 − n = −1 ⇒ n = 2.
Step 2: k = 1/(t½[A]₀) = 1/(25 × 0.40) = 0.10 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Step 3: Check: 1/(50 × 0.20) = 0.10 ✓; 1/(100 × 0.10) = 0.10 ✓.
Worked derivation: 1/[A] − 1/[A]₀ = kt with [A] = [A]₀/2 ⇒ 1/[A]₀ = kt½ ⇒ t½ = 1/(k[A]₀).
Why: For a second-order reaction the rate falls sharply as concentration falls, so starting more dilute takes proportionally longer to halve.
Why not the others: (A) First-order t½ would be constant. (C) Zero-order t½ would increase with [A]₀. (D) The t½ trend identifies the order.
Key point: t½: zero order ∝ [A]₀; first order constant; second order ∝ 1/[A]₀.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Laboratory observations with potassium permanganate and potassium dichromate: choice of acid, self-indicator action, products in neutral medium, primary standard use and colour changes
questions.question: Which set of laboratory observations and explanations for KMnO₄ and K₂Cr₂O₇ is correct?
options: A) KMnO₄ titrations are acidified with HCl, because chloride does not react with permanganate

B) Permanganate titrations are acidified with dilute H₂SO₄, not HCl, because HCl is oxidised to chlorine; KMnO₄ acts as its own indicator, since the purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺ in acid and the first permanent pink marks the end point; in neutral or faintly alkaline solution MnO₄⁻ gives brown MnO₂ and oxidises iodide to iodate; orange dichromate turns green (Cr³⁺) when it oxidises Fe²⁺ in acid; K₂Cr₂O₇ is used as a primary standard in volumetric analysis
C) KMnO₄ needs an external indicator, and dichromate is purple
D) In neutral solution MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺; K₂Cr₂O₇ is hygroscopic and cannot be weighed accurately
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) H₂SO₄ not HCl; KMnO₄ self-indicator; MnO₂ in neutral medium (I⁻ → IO₃⁻); dichromate orange → green Cr³⁺; K₂Cr₂O₇ primary standard.
Concept: Potassium dichromate is a very important chemical used in the leather industry and as an oxidant for the preparation of many azo compounds; sodium dichromate is more soluble than potassium dichromate, and the latter is prepared by treating the solution of sodium dichromate with potassium chloride; potassium dichromate is used as a primary standard in volumetric analysis. In acidic solution, its oxidising action can be represented as Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O (E° = 1.33 V); it oxidises iodide to iodine, H₂S to sulphur, and iron(II) salts to iron(III). Potassium permanganate solutions are intense purple; acidified permanganate solution oxidises oxalates to CO₂, iron(II) to iron(III), nitrites to nitrates and iodides to free iodine; in acid, MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Hydrochloric acid is not used in permanganate titrations because it is oxidised to chlorine. In neutral or faintly alkaline solutions, iodide is oxidised to iodate (2MnO₄⁻ + H₂O + I⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 2OH⁻ + IO₃⁻), thiosulphate to sulphate and manganous salt to MnO₂.
Step 1: Choice of acid: Cl⁻ would consume permanganate ⇒ use H₂SO₄.
Step 2: End point: excess purple MnO₄⁻ is visible once all reductant is used.
Step 3: Products depend on medium: acid → Mn²⁺; neutral/faintly alkaline → MnO₂.
Why: Permanganate's oxidising power and the strongly coloured reactant with nearly colourless product make it self-indicating; dichromate is stable and non-hygroscopic, so it can be weighed as a primary standard.
Why not the others: (A) HCl is oxidised by KMnO₄. (C) KMnO₄ is self-indicating; dichromate is orange. (D) Neutral medium gives MnO₂; K₂Cr₂O₇ is a primary standard.
Key point: KMnO₄: acidify with H₂SO₄, self-indicator; K₂Cr₂O₇: primary standard, orange → green.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading a table of the number of geometrical and optical isomers of square-planar and octahedral complexes, including fac/mer and cis/trans forms
questions.question:
A student tabulates stereoisomers.

Complex | Geometrical isomers | Optical isomers
[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] | 2 (cis, trans) | none
[Co(NH₃)₃(NO₂)₃] | 2 (fac, mer) | none
[Co(en)₃]³⁺ | none | 2 (d, l)
[CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ | 2 (cis, trans) | the cis form exists as d and l
[Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ | 2 (cis, trans) | none

Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) The trans isomer of [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ is optically active, giving 4 stereoisomers in all
B) [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] shows optical isomerism, because it has two kinds of ligands
C) Tetrahedral complexes commonly show geometrical isomerism

D) Every entry is correct: [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ has 3 stereoisomers in all (trans plus d- and l-cis), because the cis form is chiral while the trans form has a plane of symmetry; [Co(en)₃]³⁺ is chiral; square-planar MA₂B₂ and octahedral MA₄B₂ give cis–trans pairs; MA₃B₃ gives facial and meridional isomers; and tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism, since all positions are adjacent
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Table correct; [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺: 3 stereoisomers; tetrahedral complexes show no geometrical isomerism.
Concept: Stereoisomers have the same chemical formula and chemical bonds but different spatial arrangement; they are of two kinds, geometrical isomerism and optical isomerism. Geometrical isomerism arises in heteroleptic complexes due to different possible geometric arrangements of the ligands; in a square planar complex of formula [MX₂L₂] the two ligands X may be arranged adjacent to each other (cis) or opposite (trans); this type of isomerism also occurs in octahedral complexes of formula [MX₂L₄]. Another type of geometrical isomerism occurs in octahedral coordination entities of the type [Ma₃b₃], like [Co(NH₃)₃(NO₂)₃]: if three donor atoms of the same ligands occupy adjacent positions at the corners of an octahedral face, we have the facial (fac) isomer; when the positions are around the meridian of the octahedron, we get the meridional (mer) isomer. Tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism because the relative positions of the ligands attached to the central metal atom are the same with respect to each other. Optical isomers (enantiomers) are mirror images that cannot be superimposed on one another; optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes involving didentate ligands, e.g. [Co(en)₃]³⁺; in a complex like [PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ or [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ only the cis-isomer shows optical activity.
Given: Table entries.
Step 1: Square planar MA₂B₂: 2 geometrical, no optical (planar molecule has a mirror plane).
Step 2: [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺: trans (achiral) + cis (d and l) = 3.
Step 3: Tetrahedral: all four positions mutually adjacent ⇒ no cis/trans.
Why: Chirality needs the absence of a mirror plane; the trans arrangement and planar complexes possess one.
Why not the others: (A) The trans form has a plane of symmetry. (B) Planar complexes are achiral. (C) Tetrahedral complexes lack geometrical isomers.
Key point: cis-[M(AA)₂X₂] and [M(AA)₃] are chiral; MA₃B₃ shows fac/mer; tetrahedral shows no geometrical isomerism.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Observations when 2-bromobutane is heated with aqueous versus alcoholic KOH, applying Saytzeff's rule, and the products with KCN versus AgCN
questions.question: 2-Bromobutane is heated separately with (i) aqueous KOH and (ii) alcoholic KOH; the gas from (ii) decolourises bromine water. Bromoethane is also treated with (iii) KCN and (iv) AgCN. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) (i) gives butan-2-ol by nucleophilic substitution; (ii) gives mainly but-2-ene by dehydrohalogenation, the more substituted alkene being the major product (Saytzeff's rule), with but-1-ene as minor product; (iii) gives propanenitrile, since KCN is ionic and the cyanide ion attacks through carbon; (iv) gives ethyl isocyanide, since AgCN is mainly covalent and attacks through nitrogen
B) (i) gives but-1-ene; (ii) gives butan-2-ol
C) (ii) gives mainly but-1-ene, the less substituted alkene; (iii) and (iv) both give propanenitrile
D) Neither (i) nor (ii) reacts, because 2-bromobutane is a secondary halide
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Aqueous KOH → butan-2-ol; alcoholic KOH → mainly but-2-ene (Saytzeff); KCN → nitrile; AgCN → isocyanide.
Concept: Haloalkanes react with aqueous KOH by nucleophilic substitution, the hydroxide ion replacing the halogen to give an alcohol. When a haloalkane with a β-hydrogen atom is heated with an alcoholic solution of potassium hydroxide, there is elimination of a hydrogen atom from the β-carbon and a halogen atom from the α-carbon, so an alkene is formed (β-elimination or dehydrohalogenation). If there is a possibility of formation of more than one alkene due to the availability of more than one β-hydrogen, usually one alkene is formed as the major product; according to Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule, in dehydrohalogenation reactions the preferred product is that alkene which has the greater number of alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbon atoms. Groups like cyanides and nitrites possess two nucleophilic centres and are called ambident nucleophiles; KCN is predominantly ionic and provides cyanide ions in solution; although both carbon and nitrogen atoms are in a position to donate electron pairs, the attack takes place mainly through carbon, because the C–C bond is more stable than the C–N bond; however, AgCN is mainly covalent in nature, and nitrogen is free to donate the electron pair, forming isocyanide as the main product.
Step 1: Aqueous OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile ⇒ substitution ⇒ CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃.
Step 2: Alcoholic KOH (alkoxide, strong base) removes β-H ⇒ CH₃CH=CHCH₃ (major) + CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ (minor); the alkene decolourises bromine water.
Step 3: KCN → CH₃CH₂CN; AgCN → CH₃CH₂NC.
Why: Solvent and reagent decide the pathway: water favours substitution, alcohol favours elimination; the more substituted alkene is more stable.
Why not the others: (B) Products swapped. (C) Saytzeff gives the more substituted alkene; AgCN gives isocyanide. (D) Secondary halides react both ways.
Key point: Aqueous KOH → alcohol; alcoholic KOH → alkene (Saytzeff); KCN → RCN; AgCN → RNC.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying the carbonyl compound and Grignard reagent needed to make primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, and distinguishing the products by oxidation with acidified dichromate
questions.question: Three alcohols are prepared using CH₃MgBr followed by hydrolysis: X from methanal, Y from ethanal and Z from propanone. Each is then warmed with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. Which observation is correct?
options: A) X, Y and Z are all tertiary alcohols, so none turns the dichromate green
B) X is propan-2-ol, Y is ethanol and Z is 2-methylpropan-2-ol; all three turn dichromate green

C) X is ethanol (1°), Y is propan-2-ol (2°) and Z is 2-methylpropan-2-ol (3°); X and Y turn orange dichromate green (X giving ethanal and then ethanoic acid, Y giving propanone), while Z is not oxidised under these conditions; butanone reduced by NaBH₄ would similarly give a secondary alcohol, butan-2-ol
D) Grignard reagents add to methanal to give methanol, because no new C–C bond forms
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) X ethanol (1°), Y propan-2-ol (2°), Z 2-methylpropan-2-ol (3°); X, Y oxidised (green), Z not.
Concept: The nucleophilic addition of Grignard reagents to aldehydes and ketones results in an adduct, and hydrolysis of the adduct yields an alcohol; the overall reactions using different aldehydes and ketones are: HCHO + RMgX → RCH₂OMgX → RCH₂OH (primary alcohol); RCHO + R′MgX → secondary alcohol; R₂CO + R′MgX → tertiary alcohol. Methanal therefore gives a primary alcohol, other aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones give tertiary alcohols. Aldehydes and ketones are also reduced to the corresponding alcohols by addition of hydrogen in the presence of catalysts or by sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) or lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄); aldehydes yield primary alcohols whereas ketones give secondary alcohols. Oxidation of alcohols involves the formation of a carbon–oxygen double bond with cleavage of an O–H and a C–H bond; primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes and further to carboxylic acids, secondary alcohols to ketones, while tertiary alcohols do not undergo oxidation reaction under these conditions because they lack a hydrogen on the carbinol carbon.
Step 1: HCHO + CH₃MgBr → CH₃CH₂OMgBr → CH₃CH₂OH (X).
Step 2: CH₃CHO + CH₃MgBr → (CH₃)₂CHOH (Y); (CH₃)₂CO + CH₃MgBr → (CH₃)₃COH (Z).
Step 3: Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) → Cr³⁺ (green) only with alcohols having α-H: X and Y.
Why: The carbonyl carbon becomes the carbinol carbon, and the number of carbon groups already on it fixes the class of alcohol; oxidation needs a hydrogen on that carbon.
Why not the others: (A) Only Z is tertiary. (B) X and Y misidentified, and Z is not oxidised. (D) The methyl group adds to the carbonyl carbon, forming a C–C bond.
Key point: Grignard + HCHO → 1°, + RCHO → 2°, + R₂CO → 3°; tertiary alcohols resist dichromate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading a table of reagent combinations used to prepare ketones and checking each product, including nitriles with Grignard reagents, Friedel–Crafts acylation, dialkylcadmium and alkyne hydration
questions.question:
A table lists routes to ketones.

Row | Starting materials | Reagents | Product claimed
1 | CH₃CN | CH₃MgBr, then H₃O⁺ | propanone
2 | benzene | CH₃COCl, anhydrous AlCl₃ | acetophenone (C₆H₅COCH₃)
3 | propan-2-ol | CrO₃ (or acidified K₂Cr₂O₇) | propanone
4 | CH₃COCl | (CH₃)₂Cd | propanone
5 | propyne | dil. H₂SO₄, HgSO₄ | propanone

Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) Row 1 is wrong, because nitriles with Grignard reagents give tertiary alcohols
B) Row 4 is wrong, because acyl chlorides with dialkylcadmium give aldehydes
C) Row 5 is wrong, because propyne gives propanal by hydration

D) All five rows are correct: nitriles with Grignard reagents followed by hydrolysis give ketones; benzene undergoes Friedel–Crafts acylation; secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones; acyl chlorides react with dialkylcadmium to give ketones; and propyne is hydrated (Markovnikov) through an enol to propanone
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) All five rows give the ketones claimed.
Concept: Ketones can be prepared by: (i) treating a nitrile with a Grignard reagent followed by hydrolysis, which yields a ketone; (ii) Friedel–Crafts acylation, in which benzene or substituted benzene is treated with an acid chloride in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride to give the corresponding ketone; (iii) oxidation of secondary alcohols; (iv) treatment of acyl chlorides with dialkylcadmium, prepared by the reaction of cadmium chloride with a Grignard reagent: 2R–COCl + R′₂Cd → 2R–CO–R′ + CdCl₂; (v) hydration of alkynes: ethyne on treatment with dilute sulphuric acid and mercuric sulphate gives acetaldehyde, while all other alkynes give ketones, the addition following Markovnikov's rule via an unstable enol that tautomerises.
Given: Five rows of reagents and claimed products.
Step 1: Row 1: CH₃C≡N + CH₃MgBr → (CH₃)₂C=NMgBr → H₃O⁺ → (CH₃)₂CO.
Step 2: Row 2: C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl/AlCl₃ → C₆H₅COCH₃; Row 3: (CH₃)₂CHOH → (CH₃)₂CO.
Step 3: Row 4: 2CH₃COCl + (CH₃)₂Cd → 2CH₃COCH₃; Row 5: CH₃C≡CH + H₂O → CH₃C(OH)=CH₂ → CH₃COCH₃.
Why: Each route either forms a new C–C bond to an acyl carbon or oxidises/hydrates the correct carbon to a ketone.
Why not the others: (A) The imine salt from a nitrile hydrolyses to a ketone. (B) Dialkylcadmium gives ketones. (C) Markovnikov hydration of propyne gives propanone.
Key point: Ketones from nitrile + RMgX, Friedel–Crafts acylation, 2° alcohol oxidation, RCOCl + R′₂Cd, alkyne hydration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linking two preparations of amines from the same alkyl halide (ammonolysis and the cyanide-reduction route) to the number of carbon atoms in the product, and the reduction of nitroarenes and amides
questions.question: Bromoethane is converted to amines by two routes: (i) heating with excess ethanolic ammonia; (ii) treatment with KCN followed by reduction with LiAlH₄. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Route (i) gives ethanamine (C₂), with excess ammonia favouring the primary amine over secondary and tertiary amines and the quaternary salt; route (ii) gives propan-1-amine (C₃), because the cyanide adds one carbon before the nitrile is reduced; nitrobenzene is reduced to aniline with iron scrap and HCl, which is preferred because FeCl₂ formed is hydrolysed to release HCl, so only a small amount of acid is needed; amides are reduced by LiAlH₄ to amines with the same number of carbon atoms
B) Both routes give ethanamine
C) Route (ii) gives methanamine, because the nitrile loses a carbon on reduction
D) Route (i) gives only the quaternary ammonium salt, whatever the amount of ammonia
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (i) ethanamine (C₂); (ii) propan-1-amine (C₃); Fe/HCl for nitro reduction; LiAlH₄ reduces amides with no change in carbon count.
Concept: An alkyl or benzyl halide on reaction with an ethanolic solution of ammonia undergoes nucleophilic substitution in which the halogen atom is replaced by an amino (–NH₂) group; this process of cleavage of the C–X bond by the ammonia molecule is known as ammonolysis. The primary amine thus obtained behaves as a nucleophile and can further react with alkyl halide to form secondary and tertiary amines and finally a quaternary ammonium salt; the primary amine is obtained as a major product by taking a large excess of ammonia. Nitriles on reduction with lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄) or catalytic hydrogenation produce primary amines; this reaction is used for ascent of amine series, i.e. for preparation of amines containing one carbon atom more than the starting amine. Nitro compounds are reduced to amines by passing hydrogen gas in the presence of finely divided nickel, palladium or platinum, and also by reduction with metals in acidic medium; reduction with iron scrap and hydrochloric acid is preferred because FeCl₂ formed gets hydrolysed to release hydrochloric acid during the reaction, so only a small amount of hydrochloric acid is required to initiate the reaction. The amides on reduction with lithium aluminium hydride yield amines.
Step 1: (i) CH₃CH₂Br + NH₃ (excess) → CH₃CH₂NH₂ (2 carbons).
Step 2: (ii) CH₃CH₂Br + KCN → CH₃CH₂CN (3 carbons); LiAlH₄ → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂.
Step 3: C₆H₅NO₂ + Fe/HCl → C₆H₅NH₂; RCONH₂ + LiAlH₄ → RCH₂NH₂.
Why: Ammonolysis replaces Br by N directly; the cyanide route inserts a carbon atom between the alkyl group and nitrogen.
Why not the others: (B) Route (ii) adds a carbon. (C) Reduction of –C≡N to –CH₂NH₂ keeps every carbon. (D) Excess ammonia favours the primary amine.
Key point: R–X + NH₃ → R–NH₂ (same C); R–X → R–CN → R–CH₂NH₂ (one C more).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Why sucrose is non-reducing while maltose and lactose are reducing, what monosaccharides each gives on hydrolysis, and why hydrolysed sucrose is called invert sugar
questions.question: Which statement about disaccharides, with its reason, is correct?
options: A) Sucrose is a reducing sugar, because its glucose unit has a free aldehyde group
B) Maltose and lactose are non-reducing, because both contain two monosaccharide units

C) Sucrose is non-reducing because the glycosidic bond joins C1 of α-D-glucose with C2 of β-D-fructose, the reducing groups of both units; maltose (two α-D-glucose units, C1–C4) and lactose (β-D-galactose C1 to C4 of β-D-glucose) are reducing because one unit keeps a free hemiacetal (aldehyde-forming) carbon; maltose gives only glucose on hydrolysis, lactose gives galactose and glucose; hydrolysis turns dextrorotatory sucrose into a laevorotatory mixture, because fructose (−92.4°) rotates more strongly to the left than glucose (+52.5°) does to the right — hence "invert sugar"
D) Hydrolysis of sucrose gives two glucose molecules, so the mixture remains dextrorotatory
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Sucrose non-reducing (C1–C2 link); maltose and lactose reducing; hydrolysis products; invert sugar is laevorotatory.
Concept: Disaccharides on hydrolysis with dilute acids or enzymes yield two molecules of either the same or different monosaccharides; the two monosaccharide units are joined together by an oxide linkage formed by the loss of a water molecule, called a glycosidic linkage. In sucrose, the two monosaccharide units are held together by a glycosidic linkage between C1 of α-D-glucose and C2 of β-D-fructose; since the reducing groups of glucose and fructose are involved in glycosidic bond formation, sucrose is a non-reducing sugar. Sucrose is dextrorotatory, but after hydrolysis it gives dextrorotatory glucose and laevorotatory fructose; since the laevorotation of fructose (−92.4°) is more than the dextrorotation of glucose (+52.5°), the mixture is laevorotatory, and thus hydrolysis of sucrose brings about a change in the sign of rotation, from dextro (+) to laevo (−), and the product is named invert sugar. Maltose is composed of two α-D-glucose units in which C1 of one glucose is linked to C4 of another glucose unit; the free aldehyde group can be produced at C1 of the second glucose in solution, and it shows reducing properties, so it is a reducing sugar. Lactose (milk sugar) is composed of β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose, the linkage being between C1 of galactose and C4 of glucose; hence it is also a reducing sugar.
Step 1: A sugar is reducing if at least one anomeric carbon is free to open to the carbonyl form.
Step 2: Sucrose: both anomeric carbons used (C1 glucose, C2 fructose) ⇒ non-reducing.
Step 3: Maltose and lactose: the C4-linked glucose keeps its C1 free ⇒ reducing.
Why: The reducing test depends on a free aldehyde (or α-hydroxyketone) group, which is locked when the anomeric carbon is in the glycosidic bond.
Why not the others: (A) Glucose's C1 is used in the linkage. (B) Both keep a free anomeric carbon. (D) Sucrose gives glucose and fructose, and the mixture is laevorotatory.
Key point: Glycosidic link between both reducing carbons ⇒ non-reducing (sucrose); otherwise reducing (maltose, lactose).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Converting the composition of a glucose solution of known density into mass percentage, molality, molarity and mole fraction, and noting which terms depend on temperature
questions.question: 18.0 g of glucose (M = 180) is dissolved in 100 g of water; the solution has density 1.10 g mL⁻¹. Which set of values is correct?
options: A) Mass % = 18.0; molality = 0.100 m; molarity = 1.00 M; mole fraction of glucose = 0.10

B) Mass % = 15.3; molality = 1.00 mol kg⁻¹; molarity = 0.932 mol L⁻¹ (solution volume 118 g ÷ 1.10 g mL⁻¹ = 107.3 mL); mole fraction of glucose = 0.100/(0.100 + 5.56) = 0.0177; molarity changes with temperature because volume does, while molality and mole fraction do not
C) Mass % = 15.3; molality = 0.932 m; molarity = 1.00 M; mole fraction = 0.018
D) Mass % = 18.0; molality = 1.00 m; molarity = 1.00 M, since 1 kg of water is 1 L of solution
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 15.3 %; 1.00 m; 0.932 M; x = 0.0177.
Concept: Mass percentage of a component = mass of the component in the solution ÷ total mass of the solution × 100. Mole fraction of a component = number of moles of the component ÷ total number of moles of all the components. Molarity (M) is the number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of solution; molality (m) is the number of moles of the solute per kilogram of the solvent. Mass %, ppm, mole fraction and molality are independent of temperature, whereas molarity is a function of temperature, because volume depends on temperature and mass does not.
Given: m(glucose) = 18.0 g ⇒ 0.100 mol; m(water) = 100 g ⇒ 5.56 mol; density 1.10 g mL⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: Mass % = 100 × m_solute/m_solution; m = n/kg solvent; M = n/V(L); x = n/n_total.
Step 1: Mass of solution = 118 g ⇒ mass % = 18.0/118 × 100 = 15.3 %.
Step 2: Molality = 0.100/0.100 kg = 1.00 mol kg⁻¹; volume = 118/1.10 = 107.3 mL ⇒ molarity = 0.100/0.1073 = 0.932 mol L⁻¹.
Step 3: x(glucose) = 0.100/5.66 = 0.0177.
Why: Molality uses the solvent mass and molarity the solution volume, which includes the solute and depends on density.
Why not the others: (A) Uses solvent mass for mass % and mixes up molality and molarity. (C) Molality and molarity swapped. (D) Solution volume is not 1 L per kg of water.
Key point: Molality per kg solvent; molarity per L solution (needs density); only molarity varies with temperature.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the scalar product as work done and the projection of a force on a displacement, and splitting a force into components along and perpendicular to a direction
questions.question: A force \(\vec F=2\hat i+3\hat j-\hat k\) moves a particle from \(P(1,1,1)\) to \(Q(3,2,3)\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) Work \(=7\); component of \(\vec F\) along \(\vec{PQ}\) is \(\tfrac73\)

B) Work \(=\vec F\cdot\vec{PQ}=5\); the component of \(\vec F\) along \(\vec{PQ}\) is \(\tfrac53\); the component perpendicular to \(\vec{PQ}\) has magnitude \(\tfrac{\sqrt{101}}{3}\); the angle \(\theta\) between \(\vec F\) and \(\vec{PQ}\) satisfies \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{5}{3\sqrt{14}}\)
C) Work \(=5\); component along \(\vec{PQ}\) is \(\tfrac{5}{\sqrt{14}}\)
D) Work \(=-5\), because one component of \(\vec F\) is negative
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(W=5\); along \(\frac53\); perpendicular \(\frac{\sqrt{101}}{3}\); \(\cos\theta=\frac{5}{3\sqrt{14}}\).
Given: \(\vec F=(2,3,-1),\ \vec d=\vec{PQ}=(2,1,2),\ |\vec d|=3,\ |\vec F|=\sqrt{14}\)
Formula/Principle: \(W=\vec F\cdot\vec d;\ \text{projection of }\vec F\text{ on }\vec d=\dfrac{\vec F\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|};\ |\vec F_\perp|^2=|\vec F|^2-(\text{projection})^2\)
Step 1: \(W=2\cdot2+3\cdot1+(-1)\cdot2=5\)
Step 2: \(\text{projection}=\dfrac53\)
Step 3: \(|\vec F_\perp|=\sqrt{14-\tfrac{25}{9}}=\sqrt{\tfrac{101}{9}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{101}}{3}\)
Worked derivation: \[\cos\theta=\frac{\vec F\cdot\vec d}{|\vec F||\vec d|}=\frac{5}{3\sqrt{14}}\approx0.445\Rightarrow\theta\approx63.6^\circ\]
Check: \[\left(\tfrac53\right)^2+\tfrac{101}{9}=\tfrac{126}{9}=14=|\vec F|^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{only the part of the force along the displacement does work; the dot product picks out exactly that part times the distance}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{arithmetic error in the dot product}\); (C) \(\text{divides by }|\vec F|\text{ instead of }|\vec d|\); (D) \(\text{the total dot product is positive}\).
Key point: \(W=\vec F\cdot\vec d;\ \text{projection}=\frac{\vec F\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the locus of points equidistant from two points in space, and the ratio and point in which a coordinate plane divides the segment joining them
questions.question: For \(A(1,2,3)\) and \(B(3,2,-1)\), which statement is correct?
options: A) the locus of points equidistant from \(A\) and \(B\) is the line \(x=z\); the \(yz\)-plane divides \(AB\) internally in \(1:3\)
B) the locus is the sphere with diameter \(AB\)
C) the locus is the plane \(x+2z=5\); the \(yz\)-plane does not meet line \(AB\)

D) the locus is the plane \(x-2z=0\), which passes through the midpoint \((2,2,1)\) and is perpendicular to \(AB\); the \(yz\)-plane divides \(AB\) externally in the ratio \(1:3\), at the point \((0,2,5)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Plane \(x=2z\); \(yz\)-plane divides \(AB\) externally \(1:3\) at \((0,2,5)\).
Given: \(A(1,2,3),\ B(3,2,-1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(PA^2=PB^2;\ \text{section point }\dfrac{kB+A}{k+1}\text{ (}k<0\text{ means external)}\)
Step 1: \((x-1)^2+(y-2)^2+(z-3)^2=(x-3)^2+(y-2)^2+(z+1)^2\)
Step 2: \(-2x+1-6z+9=-6x+9+2z+1\Rightarrow4x-8z=0\Rightarrow x=2z\)
Step 3: \(x\text{-coordinate }\dfrac{3k+1}{k+1}=0\Rightarrow k=-\tfrac13\Rightarrow\text{external }1:3\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{line }AB:\ (1+2t,\ 2,\ 3-4t);\ x=0\Rightarrow t=-\tfrac12\Rightarrow(0,2,5)\]
Check: \[\text{normal }(1,0,-2)\parallel\vec{AB}=(2,0,-4)\ \checkmark;\ \text{midpoint }(2,2,1):\ 2=2\cdot1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{equidistance from two points defines the perpendicular bisecting plane; a negative ratio places the dividing point outside the segment}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the locus is a plane, and the division is external}\); (B) \(\text{the sphere on diameter }AB\text{ is where }\angle APB=90^\circ\); (C) \(\text{wrong plane; the line does meet }x=0\).
Key point: \(\text{equidistant locus}=\text{perpendicular bisector plane};\ k<0\Rightarrow\text{external division}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting elements of a Cartesian product and relations on it, and finding the domain and range of a relation defined by a parity rule
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{3,4,5\}\), and \(R=\{(a,b)\in A\times B:\ a+b\text{ is even}\}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(A\times B\) has 6 elements, so there are \(2^6=64\) relations from \(A\) to \(B\); \(R=\{(1,3),(1,5),(2,4)\}\), with domain \(\{1,2\}\) and range \(\{3,4,5\}\); \(A\times B\ne B\times A\) because \((1,3)\in A\times B\) but \((1,3)\notin B\times A\)
B) \(A\times B\) has 5 elements and 32 relations; \(R\) has domain \(\{1\}\)
C) \(A\times B=B\times A\), since both have 6 elements
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(|A\times B|=6\); \(64\) relations; \(R=\{(1,3),(1,5),(2,4)\}\); domain \(\{1,2\}\), range \(\{3,4,5\}\).
Given: \(A=\{1,2\},\ B=\{3,4,5\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(|A\times B|=|A||B|;\ \text{relations}=\text{subsets of }A\times B:\ 2^{|A||B|}\)
Step 1: \(|A\times B|=2\times3=6\Rightarrow2^6=64\text{ relations}\)
Step 2: \(a=1:\ b\text{ odd}\Rightarrow3,5;\ a=2:\ b\text{ even}\Rightarrow4\)
Step 3: \(\text{domain}=\{1,2\},\ \text{range}=\{3,4,5\}\)
Worked derivation: \[A\times B=\{(1,3),(1,4),(1,5),(2,3),(2,4),(2,5)\}\]
Check: \[(1,3)\in B\times A\text{ would need }1\in B\ \times\]
Why: \(\text{a relation is any subset of the Cartesian product; ordered pairs depend on order, so }A\times B\text{ and }B\times A\text{ differ}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{miscounts}\); (C) \(\text{equal size does not mean equal sets}\); (D) \(\text{these pairs have odd sums}\).
Key point: \(|A\times B|=pq;\ \text{relations}=2^{pq}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the parameters of a function from its given domain, and the range of a rational function
questions.question: The real function \(f(x)=\sqrt{\dfrac{x-a}{b-x}}\) has domain \([2,5)\). Which statement is correct?
options: B) \(a=2,\ b=5\); range of \(f\) is \((0,\infty)\)

C) \(a=2,\ b=5\), since \(\dfrac{x-2}{5-x}\ge0\) exactly for \(2\le x<5\) (\(x=5\) excluded as it makes the denominator zero); the range of \(f\) is \([0,\infty)\); and \(g(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2+1}\) has range \((0,1]\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(a=2,\ b=5\); range \([0,\infty)\); \(g\) has range \((0,1]\).
Given: \(\text{domain of }f=[2,5)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sqrt{u}\text{ real}\Leftrightarrow u\ge0;\ \text{denominator}\ne0\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{x-a}{b-x}\ge0\text{ with }a<b\Leftrightarrow a\le x<b\)
Step 2: \(\text{matching }[2,5):\ a=2,\ b=5\)
Step 3: \(\text{as }x\to5^-,\ f\to\infty;\ f(2)=0\Rightarrow\text{range }[0,\infty)\)
Worked derivation: \[g:\ x^2+1\ge1\Rightarrow0<\frac{1}{x^2+1}\le1,\ \text{max }1\text{ at }x=0,\ \text{never }0\]
Check: \[x=3:\ \sqrt{1/2}\text{ real}\ \checkmark;\quad x=1:\ \sqrt{-1/4}\text{ not real}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the closed end comes from the numerator vanishing, the open end from the denominator vanishing}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{gives domain }(2,5]\text{ reversed}\); (B) \(f(2)=0\text{ is included}\); (D) \(g\text{ never reaches }0\).
Key point: \(\frac{x-a}{b-x}\ge0\Leftrightarrow a\le x<b\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Converting between radians and degrees for arcs and angular speeds, and finding the other trigonometric ratios from one ratio and the quadrant
questions.question: A wheel makes 360 revolutions per minute; an arc of 22 cm lies on a circle of radius 100 cm; and \(\sin x=-\tfrac35\) with \(x\) in the third quadrant. Which set of results about angular speed, the angle subtended and the other trigonometric ratios is correct?
options: A) A wheel making 360 revolutions per minute turns through \(6\pi\) rad/s; an arc of 22 cm on a circle of radius 100 cm subtends \(22^\circ\)
B) If \(\sin x=-\tfrac35\) and \(x\) is in the third quadrant, \(\cos x=\tfrac45\) and \(\tan x=-\tfrac34\)

C) A wheel making 360 revolutions per minute turns through \(12\pi\) rad/s; an arc of 22 cm on a circle of radius 100 cm subtends \(0.22\) rad \(\approx12^\circ36'\) (using \(\pi=\tfrac{22}{7}\)); if \(\sin x=-\tfrac35\) with \(x\) in the third quadrant, then \(\cos x=-\tfrac45\) and \(\tan x=\tfrac34\)
D) An arc of 22 cm on radius 100 cm subtends \(\tfrac{100}{22}\) rad
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(12\pi\) rad/s; \(0.22\) rad \(\approx12^\circ36'\); \(\cos x=-\frac45,\ \tan x=\frac34\).
Given: \(360\ \text{rev/min};\ l=22\ \text{cm},\ r=100\ \text{cm};\ \sin x=-\tfrac35,\ \pi<x<\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\theta=\dfrac lr;\ 1\ \text{rev}=2\pi\ \text{rad};\ 1\ \text{rad}=\dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}\)
Step 1: \(360\ \text{rev/min}=6\ \text{rev/s}=12\pi\ \text{rad/s}\)
Step 2: \(\theta=\dfrac{22}{100}=0.22\ \text{rad}=0.22\times\dfrac{180\times7}{22}=12.6^\circ=12^\circ36'\)
Step 3: \(\cos^2x=1-\tfrac{9}{25}=\tfrac{16}{25};\ \text{third quadrant}\Rightarrow\cos x=-\tfrac45,\ \tan x=\dfrac{-3/5}{-4/5}=\tfrac34\)
Worked derivation: \[\sin^2x+\cos^2x=\tfrac{9}{25}+\tfrac{16}{25}=1\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{third quadrant: sine and cosine negative, tangent positive}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the radian is defined as arc length over radius; quadrant signs fix the sign of the square root}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgets }2\pi\text{ per revolution and confuses radians with degrees}\); (B) \(\text{cosine is negative in the third quadrant}\); (D) \(\text{ratio inverted}\).
Key point: \(\theta=l/r;\ \text{third quadrant: only tan positive}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Simplifying a quotient of complex numbers to a + ib and finding its modulus, conjugate, square and reciprocal
questions.question: For \(z=\dfrac{3+4i}{1-2i}\), which set of results is correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(z=-1+2i,\ |z|=\sqrt5,\ \bar z=-1-2i,\ z^2=-3-4i,\ \frac1z=\frac{-1-2i}{5}\).
Given: \(z=\dfrac{3+4i}{1-2i}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{multiply by the conjugate of the denominator};\ |z_1/z_2|=|z_1|/|z_2|;\ \dfrac1z=\dfrac{\bar z}{|z|^2}\)
Step 1: \(z=\dfrac{(3+4i)(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)}=\dfrac{3+6i+4i+8i^2}{1+4}=\dfrac{-5+10i}{5}=-1+2i\)
Step 2: \(|z|=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt5;\ \text{check }\dfrac{|3+4i|}{|1-2i|}=\dfrac{5}{\sqrt5}=\sqrt5\)
Step 3: \(z^2=1-4i+4i^2=-3-4i;\ \dfrac1z=\dfrac{-1-2i}{5}\)
Worked derivation: \[z\cdot\frac1z=\frac{(-1+2i)(-1-2i)}{5}=\frac{1+4}{5}=1\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[|z^2|=|-3-4i|=5=|z|^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{multiplying by the conjugate makes the denominator real, giving the standard form}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{sign and modulus errors}\); (C) \(\text{multiplied incorrectly}\); (D) \(z^2\ne z\bar z\).
Key point: \(z\bar z=|z|^2;\ 1/z=\bar z/|z|^2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting shortest lattice paths in three dimensions as permutations of letters with repetition, including paths through a given point
questions.question: A particle moves from \((0,0,0)\) to \((2,2,1)\) by unit steps in the positive \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\) direction. How many shortest paths are there, and how many pass through \((1,1,0)\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(30\) paths; \(12\) through \((1,1,0)\).
Given: \(\text{target }(2,2,1);\ \text{steps }X,Y,Z\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{a path is an arrangement of }XXYYZ:\ \dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!\,r!}\)
Step 1: \(\text{total}=\dfrac{5!}{2!\,2!\,1!}=\dfrac{120}{4}=30\)
Step 2: \((0,0,0)\to(1,1,0):\ \text{arrangements of }XY=2\)
Step 3: \((1,1,0)\to(2,2,1):\ \text{arrangements of }XYZ=3!=6\Rightarrow2\times6=12\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{paths through }(1,1,0)=\frac{2!}{1!1!}\cdot\frac{3!}{1!1!1!}=12\]
Check: \[12\le30\ \checkmark;\ \text{2D analogue }(2,2):\ \tfrac{4!}{2!2!}=6\]
Why: \(\text{each shortest path is a word made of the required numbers of each step, so counting paths is counting permutations with repetition}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores repeated steps}\); (B) \(\text{multiplies coordinates}\); (C) \(\text{ignores the }z\text{ step}\).
Key point: \(\text{paths to }(a,b,c)=\frac{(a+b+c)!}{a!\,b!\,c!}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the formulas for Σk, Σk² and Σk³, the identity Σk³ = (Σk)², and the limiting value of Σk²/n³
questions.question: Which statement about special sums is correct?
options: C) \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\sum k^2}{n^3}=\frac12\)
D) \(\sum k^3=\left(\sum k^2\right)^2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(3025=55^2\); \(385\); limit \(\frac13\); odd sum \(n^2\).
Given: \(n=10\text{ and general }n\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sum k=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2};\ \sum k^2=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6};\ \sum k^3=\left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2\)
Step 1: \(\sum_{1}^{10}k=55;\ \sum_{1}^{10}k^3=55^2=3025\)
Step 2: \(\sum_{1}^{10}k^2=\dfrac{10\cdot11\cdot21}{6}=385\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n^3}=\dfrac{(1+1/n)(2+1/n)}{6}\to\dfrac{2}{6}=\dfrac13\)
Worked derivation: \[\sum_{k=1}^{n}(2k-1)=2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}-n=n^2\]
Check: \[n=2:\ 1+8=9=(1+2)^2\ \checkmark;\ 1+4=5=\tfrac{2\cdot3\cdot5}{6}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the sum of cubes equals the square of the sum, and the leading term of }\sum k^2\text{ is }n^3/3\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{confuses }10^3\text{ and }10^2\text{ with the sums}\); (C) \(\text{that is }\lim\sum k/n^2\); (D) \(\text{it is }(\sum k)^2\).
Key point: \(\sum k^3=(\sum k)^2;\ \sum k^2\sim n^3/3\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding all lines through a given point whose intercepts on the axes have a given sum, using the intercept form
questions.question: Which lines pass through \((3,4)\) and have intercepts on the axes whose sum is 14?
options: B) only \(x+y=7\)
D) no such line exists
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(4x+3y=24\) and \(x+y=7\).
Given: \(\text{point }(3,4);\ a+b=14\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac xa+\dfrac yb=1\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac3a+\dfrac{4}{14-a}=1\Rightarrow3(14-a)+4a=a(14-a)\)
Step 2: \(42+a=14a-a^2\Rightarrow a^2-13a+42=0\Rightarrow(a-6)(a-7)=0\)
Step 3: \(a=6,\ b=8:\ \dfrac x6+\dfrac y8=1\Rightarrow4x+3y=24;\quad a=7,\ b=7:\ x+y=7\)
Worked derivation: \[(3,4):\ 12+12=24\ \checkmark;\quad3+4=7\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{intercept sums: }6+8=14,\ 7+7=14\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the point condition and the sum condition give a quadratic in }a\text{, and each real root gives one line}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{misses }a=6\); (C) \(\text{intercept sums wrong}\); (D) \(\text{the quadratic has real roots}\).
Key point: \(\text{intercept form }\frac xa+\frac yb=1\text{; two conditions fix }a,b\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the circle through three points including the origin, its centre and radius, and the tangent at the origin
questions.question: What is the circle through \((0,0)\), \((4,0)\) and \((0,6)\), and which accompanying statement is correct?
options: D) \(x^2+y^2-4x-6y=0\), centre \((2,3)\), radius \(\sqrt{13}\); the segment joining \((4,0)\) and \((0,6)\) is a diameter since it subtends a right angle at the origin; the tangent at the origin is \(2x+3y=0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(x^2+y^2-4x-6y=0\); centre \((2,3)\); \(r=\sqrt{13}\); tangent \(2x+3y=0\).
Given: \(\text{points }(0,0),(4,0),(0,6)\)
Formula/Principle: \(x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0;\ \text{centre }(-g,-f),\ r=\sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}\)
Step 1: \((0,0)\Rightarrow c=0\)
Step 2: \((4,0)\Rightarrow16+8g=0\Rightarrow g=-2;\ (0,6)\Rightarrow36+12f=0\Rightarrow f=-3\)
Step 3: \(\text{centre }(2,3),\ r=\sqrt{4+9}=\sqrt{13}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{tangent at origin}\perp\text{radius }(2,3):\ 2x+3y=0\]
Check: \[\text{midpoint of }(4,0),(0,6)=(2,3);\ \text{half-length}=\tfrac12\sqrt{16+36}=\sqrt{13}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{three non-collinear points fix }g,f,c\text{; the right angle at the origin makes the hypotenuse a diameter}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{does not pass through the origin}\); (B) \(\text{signs wrong}\); (C) \(\text{misses factor 2}\).
Key point: \(\text{circle through origin: }c=0;\ \text{tangent}\perp\text{radius}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding a parabola y² = 4ax through a given point, its focus, directrix and latus rectum, and the value of c for which y = mx + c touches it
questions.question: The parabola \(y^2=4ax\) passes through \((2,-4)\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(a=-2\); focus \((-2,0)\); the line \(y=x+k\) touches it for \(k=-2\)
B) \(a=2\): focus \((2,0)\), directrix \(x=-2\), latus rectum 8; the line \(y=x+k\) touches the parabola exactly when \(k=\dfrac am=2\), at the point \((2,4)\)
C) \(a=8\); latus rectum 32; tangent for \(k=8\)
D) \(a=2\); focus \((0,2)\); directrix \(y=-2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(a=2\); focus \((2,0)\); directrix \(x=-2\); LR \(8\); \(k=2\), touching at \((2,4)\).
Given: \((2,-4)\text{ on }y^2=4ax;\ \text{line }y=x+k\)
Formula/Principle: \(y^2=4ax:\ \text{focus }(a,0),\ \text{directrix }x=-a,\ \text{LR}=4a;\ y=mx+c\text{ tangent}\Leftrightarrow c=\dfrac am\)
Step 1: \(16=8a\Rightarrow a=2\Rightarrow y^2=8x\)
Step 2: \(\text{focus }(2,0),\ \text{directrix }x=-2,\ \text{LR}=8\)
Step 3: \((x+k)^2=8x\Rightarrow x^2+(2k-8)x+k^2=0;\ \text{double root}\Leftrightarrow(2k-8)^2=4k^2\Rightarrow k=2\)
Worked derivation: \[k=2:\ x^2-4x+4=0\Rightarrow x=2,\ y=4\]
Check: \[(2,4):\ 16=8\cdot2\ \checkmark;\ \text{distance to focus }4=\text{distance to directrix }4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a line touches a conic when substitution gives a repeated root (zero discriminant)}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(a\text{ must be positive since }16=8a\); (C) \(\text{wrong }a\); (D) \(\text{focus and directrix belong to }x^2=4ay\).
Key point: \(y^2=4ax:\ \text{tangent }y=mx+\frac am\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using standard exponential and logarithmic limits to find the parameter that makes a limit take a given value
questions.question: For which \(k\) is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{kx}-1}{\ln(1+3x)}=2\), and what then is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}(1+x)^{k/x}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(k=6\); \(e^6\).
Given: \(\text{limit }=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1}{x}=1,\ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln(1+x)}{x}=1,\ \lim_{x\to0}(1+x)^{1/x}=e\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{e^{kx}-1}{\ln(1+3x)}=\dfrac{e^{kx}-1}{kx}\cdot\dfrac{3x}{\ln(1+3x)}\cdot\dfrac{k}{3}\to\dfrac k3\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac k3=2\Rightarrow k=6\)
Step 3: \((1+x)^{6/x}=\left[(1+x)^{1/x}\right]^6\to e^6\)
Worked derivation: \[x=0.001:\ \frac{e^{0.006}-1}{\ln1.003}\approx\frac{0.006018}{0.0029955}\approx2.009\]
Check: \[\text{series: }\frac{kx+\cdots}{3x+\cdots}\to\frac k3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{near 0 both numerator and denominator behave linearly, so the limit is the ratio of their slopes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ratio inverted}\); (B) \(\text{ignores the factor 3}\); (D) \((1+x)^{6/x}\text{ is a }1^\infty\text{ form, not 1}\).
Key point: \(\frac{e^{kx}-1}{\ln(1+mx)}\to\frac km\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting outcomes and events in the sample space of two dice, mutually exclusive events, and the number of possible events of a finite sample space
questions.question: Two fair dice are thrown. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The sample space has 12 outcomes; "sum 7" has 7 outcomes
B) "Sum 7" and "doubles" are not mutually exclusive

C) The sample space has 36 outcomes; "sum is 7" has 6 outcomes and "doubles" has 6, and these two events are mutually exclusive (no double sums to 7); "at least one six" has 11 outcomes; and any sample space with 3 outcomes has \(2^3=8\) possible events (subsets)
D) "At least one six" has 12 outcomes, since each die can show a six in 6 ways
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(36\); sum 7: \(6\); doubles: \(6\); mutually exclusive; at least one six: \(11\); \(2^3=8\) events.
Given: \(\text{two dice};\ S=\{(i,j):1\le i,j\le6\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(|S|=6\times6;\ \text{complement};\ \text{events}=\text{subsets of }S\Rightarrow2^{|S|}\)
Step 1: \(|S|=36;\ \text{sum 7}:\ (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1)\Rightarrow6\)
Step 2: \(\text{doubles }(k,k):\ 6;\ 2k=7\text{ impossible}\Rightarrow\text{disjoint}\)
Step 3: \(\text{no six}:\ 5\times5=25\Rightarrow\text{at least one six}=36-25=11\)
Worked derivation: \[|A\cup B|=6+6-0=12\text{ for sum 7 or doubles}\]
Check: \[\text{direct count: 6 with first die six}+6\text{ with second}-1\text{ for }(6,6)=11\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{ordered pairs make all 36 outcomes equally likely; complements avoid double counting}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ordered pairs give 36}\); (B) \(\text{no outcome is in both}\); (D) \((6,6)\text{ counted twice}\).
Key point: \(|S|=36;\ \text{at least one}=\text{total}-\text{none};\ \text{events}=2^{|S|}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Evaluating principal values of sin⁻¹(sin x), cos⁻¹(cos x) and tan⁻¹(tan x) for angles outside the principal ranges, and the zig-zag graph of sin⁻¹(sin x)
questions.question: Using principal values, what are \(\sin^{-1}\!\left(\sin\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\), \(\cos^{-1}\!\left(\cos\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\) and \(\tan^{-1}\!\left(\tan\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)\), in that order?
options: A) \(\tfrac{\pi}{3},\ \tfrac{5\pi}{6},\ -\tfrac{\pi}{4}\); the graph of \(y=\sin^{-1}(\sin x)\) is a zig-zag of slope \(\pm1\), equal to \(\pi-x\) for \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\)
B) \(\tfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \tfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \tfrac{3\pi}{4}\)
C) \(\tfrac{\pi}{3},\ -\tfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \tfrac{\pi}{4}\)
D) \(-\tfrac{\pi}{3},\ \tfrac{\pi}{6},\ -\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\frac{\pi}{3},\ \frac{5\pi}{6},\ -\frac{\pi}{4}\).
Given: \(\text{principal ranges: }\sin^{-1}\in[-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2],\ \cos^{-1}\in[0,\pi],\ \tan^{-1}\in(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{find the angle in the principal range with the same function value}\)
Step 1: \(\sin\tfrac{2\pi}{3}=\sin\left(\pi-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=\sin\tfrac{\pi}{3},\ \tfrac\pi3\in\text{range}\Rightarrow\tfrac\pi3\)
Step 2: \(\cos\tfrac{7\pi}{6}=\cos\left(2\pi-\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)=\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \tfrac{5\pi}{6}\in[0,\pi]\Rightarrow\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\)
Step 3: \(\tan\tfrac{3\pi}{4}=\tan\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{4}-\pi\right)=\tan\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\Rightarrow-\tfrac\pi4\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{for }\tfrac\pi2\le x\le\tfrac{3\pi}{2}:\ \sin^{-1}(\sin x)=\pi-x;\ x=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\Rightarrow\tfrac\pi3\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{6}=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=\cos\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{inverse functions return only principal values, so the angle must be moved into the principal range using symmetry or periodicity}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{outside the principal ranges}\); (C) \(\cos^{-1}\text{ is never negative; tan value sign wrong}\); (D) \(\text{signs wrong}\).
Key point: \(\sin^{-1}(\sin x)=x\text{ only for }x\in[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2]\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the values of a parameter for which a 3×3 matrix is invertible, computing its adjoint and inverse, and the determinant of the adjoint
questions.question: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&k&3\\1&3&3\\1&3&4\end{pmatrix}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(A\) is invertible for every \(k\)

B) \(|A|=3-k\), so \(A\) is invertible iff \(k\ne3\); for \(k=2\), \(|A|=1\) and \(A^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&-3\\-1&1&0\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}\); in general \(A(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|I\) and \(|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^2\)
C) \(|A|=k-3\); for \(k=2\), \(A^{-1}=-\operatorname{adj}A\)
D) \(|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^3\) for a \(3\times3\) matrix
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(|A|=3-k\); invertible iff \(k\ne3\); for \(k=2\), \(A^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}A\).
Given: \(A\text{ as stated}\)
Formula/Principle: \(A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj}A;\ |\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}\)
Step 1: \(|A|=1(12-9)-k(4-3)+3(3-3)=3-k\)
Step 2: \(k=2:\ \text{cofactors }C_{11}=3,C_{12}=-1,C_{13}=0;\ C_{21}=1,C_{22}=1,C_{23}=-1;\ C_{31}=-3,C_{32}=0,C_{33}=1\)
Step 3: \(\operatorname{adj}A=\text{transpose of cofactor matrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&-3\\-1&1&0\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}\)
Worked derivation: \[\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\1&3&3\\1&3&4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3&1&-3\\-1&1&0\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\]
Check: \[|\operatorname{adj}A|=3(1)-1(-1)+(-3)(1)=1=|A|^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a square matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is non-zero}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k=3\text{ makes }|A|=0\); (C) \(\text{sign error}\); (D) \(|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}=|A|^2\).
Key point: \(A^{-1}\text{ exists}\Leftrightarrow|A|\ne0;\ |\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using logarithmic differentiation on a product–quotient of powers and finding the exponent that makes the derivative vanish at a point
questions.question: Let \(y=\dfrac{(x+1)^2(x+2)^3}{(x+3)^k}\). For which \(k\) is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0\) at \(x=0\)?
options: B) \(k=\tfrac72\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(k=\frac{21}{2}\).
Given: \(y=\dfrac{(x+1)^2(x+2)^3}{(x+3)^k}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\ln y=2\ln(x+1)+3\ln(x+2)-k\ln(x+3)\Rightarrow\dfrac{y'}{y}=\dfrac{2}{x+1}+\dfrac{3}{x+2}-\dfrac{k}{x+3}\)
Step 1: \(\text{at }x=0:\ \dfrac{y'}{y}=2+\dfrac32-\dfrac k3\)
Step 2: \(y(0)=\dfrac{8}{3^k}\ne0\Rightarrow y'(0)=0\Leftrightarrow2+\dfrac32-\dfrac k3=0\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac k3=\dfrac72\Rightarrow k=\dfrac{21}{2}\)
Worked derivation: \[k=\tfrac{21}{2}:\ \frac{y'}{y}\Big|_0=\frac{7}{2}-\frac{21}{6}=0\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{for }k=0:\ y'(0)=8\left(2+\tfrac32\right)=28\ne0\]
Why: \(\text{taking logs turns products and powers into sums, so the derivative separates into simple terms}\)
Why not the others: (A),(B),(C) \(\text{come from dropping the factor 3 or mis-adding }2+\tfrac32\).
Key point: \(\text{log differentiation: }y'=y\sum\frac{n_i}{x-a_i}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Rates of change of the volume and surface area of a spherical balloon whose radius grows at a constant rate, and how they scale with radius
questions.question: The radius of a spherical balloon increases at 0.5 cm/s. At the instant the radius is 10 cm, which statement is correct?
options: A) Volume increases at \(50\pi\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}\) and area at \(20\pi\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\)

B) Volume increases at \(200\pi\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}\) and surface area at \(40\pi\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\); when the radius is 20 cm the volume rate is 4 times larger, while at the start (\(r\to0\)) both rates are nearly zero even though the radius grows steadily
C) Volume increases at \(\tfrac{2000\pi}{3}\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}\)
D) Both rates are constant, because \(\dfrac{dr}{dt}\) is constant
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\frac{dV}{dt}=200\pi\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}\); \(\frac{dS}{dt}=40\pi\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\).
Given: \(\dfrac{dr}{dt}=0.5\ \text{cm/s},\ r=10\ \text{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(V=\tfrac43\pi r^3,\ S=4\pi r^2;\ \text{chain rule}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\dfrac{dr}{dt}=4\pi(100)(0.5)=200\pi\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=8\pi r\dfrac{dr}{dt}=8\pi(10)(0.5)=40\pi\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}\propto r^2\Rightarrow r=20\text{ gives }4\times\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dV/dt}{dS/dt}=\frac{4\pi r^2}{8\pi r}=\frac r2=5\ \text{cm}\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{units: cm}^2\times\text{cm/s}=\text{cm}^3/\text{s}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a thin shell of thickness }dr\text{ adds volume }4\pi r^2dr\text{, so the same }dr\text{ adds more volume on a bigger balloon}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }r\text{ instead of }r^2\); (C) \(\text{uses }V/r\times dr/dt\text{ instead of }4\pi r^2\,dr/dt\); (D) \(\text{rates depend on }r\).
Key point: \(\frac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Evaluating definite integrals with quadratic denominators by completing the square, and a square-root integral interpreted as the area of a quarter circle
questions.question: Which pair of values is correct for \(I_1=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{dx}{x^2+2x+5}\) and \(I_2=\displaystyle\int_0^2\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx\)?
options: D) \(I_1=\tfrac{\pi}{8}\), from \(\tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac{x+1}{2}\); \(I_2=\pi\), the area of a quarter of the circle \(x^2+y^2=4\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(I_1=\frac{\pi}{8}\); \(I_2=\pi\).
Given: \(x^2+2x+5=(x+1)^2+4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{u^2+a^2}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac ua;\ \int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=\frac x2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}+\frac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac xa\)
Step 1: \(I_1=\left[\tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac{x+1}{2}\right]_{-1}^{1}=\tfrac12\left(\tan^{-1}1-\tan^{-1}0\right)\)
Step 2: \(I_1=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{4}=\tfrac{\pi}{8}\)
Step 3: \(I_2=\left[\tfrac x2\sqrt{4-x^2}+2\sin^{-1}\tfrac x2\right]_0^2=0+2\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{2}=\pi\)
Worked derivation: \[y=\sqrt{4-x^2},\ 0\le x\le2:\ \text{quarter disc of radius 2, area }\tfrac14\pi(2)^2=\pi\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[I_1\approx0.393;\ \text{integrand between }\tfrac18\text{ and }\tfrac14\text{ on an interval of length 2}\Rightarrow0.25<I_1<0.5\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{completing the square turns the quadratic into the standard }u^2+a^2\text{ form; the square-root integrand traces a circle}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses the factor }\tfrac12\text{ and doubles the area}\); (B) \(\text{wrong forms}\); (C) \(\text{the denominator has no real roots, so no logarithm}\).
Key point: \(\int\frac{dx}{(x+b)^2+a^2}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac{x+b}{a}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to find where an integral-defined function increases, decreases and has extrema, and sketching its behaviour
questions.question: Let \(F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x(t^2-4t+3)\,dt\) for \(x\ge0\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(F'(x)=x^2-4x+3\), so \(F\) has a local maximum \(F(1)=\tfrac43\) and a local minimum \(F(3)=0\); in fact \(F(x)=\tfrac x3(x-3)^2\ge0\) for \(x\ge0\), touching zero at \(x=0\) and \(x=3\)
B) \(F'(x)=2x-4\); minimum at \(x=2\)
C) \(F\) has a local minimum at \(x=1\) and a maximum at \(x=3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Local max \(\frac43\) at \(x=1\); local min \(0\) at \(x=3\); \(F(x)=\frac x3(x-3)^2\).
Given: \(F(x)=\int_0^x(t^2-4t+3)\,dt\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{FTC: }F'(x)=f(x);\ \text{sign of }F'\text{ gives monotonicity}\)
Step 1: \(F'(x)=x^2-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3)\)
Step 2: \(F'>0\text{ on }(0,1),\ <0\text{ on }(1,3),\ >0\text{ on }(3,\infty)\Rightarrow\text{max at }1,\ \text{min at }3\)
Step 3: \(F(x)=\tfrac{x^3}{3}-2x^2+3x\Rightarrow F(1)=\tfrac13-2+3=\tfrac43,\ F(3)=9-18+9=0\)
Worked derivation: \[F(x)=\frac x3\left(x^2-6x+9\right)=\frac x3(x-3)^2\]
Check: \[F''(x)=2x-4:\ F''(1)=-2<0\ (\max),\ F''(3)=2>0\ (\min)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the FTC turns questions about an accumulated area into questions about its integrand, whose sign shows when area is being added or removed}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{differentiates the integrand instead}\); (C) \(\text{reversed}\); (D) \(\text{values swapped}\).
Key point: \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^xf(t)\,dt=f(x)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Determining the order and degree of several differential equations, recognising when the degree is not defined, and the number of arbitrary constants in general and particular solutions
questions.question: Consider (i) \(\left(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^3+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^4+y=0\); (ii) \(\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}+\sin\!\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)=0\); (iii) \(\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2=1+x\); (iv) \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) All four have a defined degree; (ii) has degree 1
B) (i) has order 3 and degree 2

C) Degree is defined for exactly three of them: (i) order 2, degree 3; (iii) order 1, degree 2; (iv) order 2, degree 2 after squaring to make it polynomial in the derivatives; (ii) has order 3 but no defined degree, since it is not a polynomial in \(y'\); the general solution of an \(n\)th-order equation has \(n\) arbitrary constants, while a particular solution has none
D) Degree is defined for exactly two of them, because (iv) contains a square root
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Three have a defined degree: (i) 2, 3; (iii) 1, 2; (iv) 2, 2; (ii) undefined.
Given: \(\text{equations (i)–(iv)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{order}=\text{highest derivative};\ \text{degree}=\text{power of the highest derivative when the equation is a polynomial in derivatives}\)
Step 1: \(\text{(i) highest }y''\text{, power 3}\Rightarrow\text{order 2, degree 3}\)
Step 2: \(\text{(ii) }\sin(y')\text{ is not polynomial}\Rightarrow\text{degree undefined, order 3};\ \text{(iii) order 1, degree 2}\)
Step 3: \(\text{(iv) }(y'')^2=1+(y')^2\Rightarrow\text{order 2, degree 2}\)
Worked derivation: \[y''+y=0:\ y=A\cos x+B\sin x\ (2\text{ constants});\ y(0)=0,\ y'(0)=1\Rightarrow y=\sin x\ (\text{particular})\]
Check: \[\text{count of defined degrees}=3\ (\text{i, iii, iv})\]
Why: \(\text{degree needs the equation to be polynomial in the derivatives; radicals can be cleared, transcendental functions cannot}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{(ii) has no degree}\); (B) \(\text{order 2, degree 3}\); (D) \(\text{the root in (iv) can be cleared}\).
Key point: \(\text{degree defined only for polynomial equations in derivatives}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing linear expansion of rails, a bimetallic strip and volume expansion, and the anomalous expansion of water near 4 °C
questions.question: Steel (\(\alpha=1.2\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\)) rails 10 m long are laid at 10 °C; the hottest expected rail temperature is 50 °C. A brass–steel bimetallic strip (\(\alpha_{\text{brass}}=1.9\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\)) is straight at room temperature. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Each rail needs a gap of at least 4.8 mm; on heating, the bimetallic strip bends with brass on the outer (convex) side because brass expands more; the volume expansion coefficient of steel is about \(3\alpha=3.6\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\); water, unusually, contracts on heating from 0 °C to 4 °C, where its density is maximum
B) The gap needed is 0.48 mm; the strip bends with steel outside
C) The gap needed is 48 mm; \(\gamma=\alpha/3\)
D) No gap is needed, because steel does not expand appreciably; water expands steadily from 0 °C
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Gap \(4.8\) mm; brass on the convex side; \(\gamma\approx3\alpha\); water densest at 4 °C.
Given: \(L=10\ \mathrm m,\ \alpha=1.2\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}},\ \Delta T=40\ \mathrm K\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta L=L\alpha\Delta T;\ \gamma=3\alpha\text{ for isotropic solids}\)
Step 1: \(\Delta L=10\times1.2\times10^{-5}\times40=4.8\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m=4.8\ \mathrm{mm}\)
Step 2: \(\text{brass expands more}\Rightarrow\text{longer side on the outside of the curve}\)
Step 3: \(\gamma=3\times1.2\times10^{-5}=3.6\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\)
Worked derivation: \[V=L^3(1+\alpha\Delta T)^3\approx L^3(1+3\alpha\Delta T)\Rightarrow\gamma=3\alpha\]
Check: \[\frac{\Delta L}{L}=4.8\times10^{-4}\ \text{(small, so linear approximation valid)}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{rails expand freely only if a gap is left; otherwise the large thermal stress buckles them}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{factor 10 error; brass is outside}\); (C) \(\text{factor 10 error; }\gamma=3\alpha\); (D) \(\text{4.8 mm is significant; water contracts from 0 to 4 °C}\).
Key point: \(\Delta L=L\alpha\Delta T;\ \gamma=3\alpha;\ \text{water densest at }4\ ^\circ\mathrm C\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Efficiency, work and rejected heat of a Carnot engine between two reservoirs, and recognising isothermal and adiabatic curves on its P–V diagram
questions.question: A Carnot engine works between 750 K and 300 K and absorbs 2000 J per cycle from the hot reservoir. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Efficiency 40 %; work 800 J; on the P–V diagram the isothermal curves are steeper than the adiabatic ones
B) Efficiency 100 %, since the engine is reversible

C) Efficiency \(1-\tfrac{300}{750}=60\ \%\); work per cycle 1200 J; heat rejected 800 J; its P–V diagram consists of two isotherms joined by two adiabats, the adiabats being steeper (\(PV^\gamma\) = constant, \(\gamma>1\)); by the Kelvin–Planck statement, no engine can turn all the absorbed heat into work
D) Efficiency 60 %; heat rejected 1200 J
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\eta=60\%\); \(W=1200\) J; \(Q_2=800\) J; adiabats steeper.
Given: \(T_1=750\ \mathrm K,\ T_2=300\ \mathrm K,\ Q_1=2000\ \mathrm J\)
Formula/Principle: \(\eta=1-\dfrac{T_2}{T_1};\ W=\eta Q_1;\ Q_2=Q_1-W\)
Step 1: \(\eta=1-\dfrac{300}{750}=0.60\)
Step 2: \(W=0.60\times2000=1200\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(Q_2=2000-1200=800\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}=\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{800}{2000}=0.40\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{isotherm slope }-\tfrac PV;\ \text{adiabat slope }-\gamma\tfrac PV\Rightarrow\text{adiabat steeper}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a Carnot engine is reversible, so its efficiency depends only on the reservoir temperatures and is the maximum possible}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{efficiency wrong; adiabats are steeper}\); (B) \(\text{violates the second law}\); (D) \(\text{work and rejected heat swapped}\).
Key point: \(\eta_{\text{Carnot}}=1-T_2/T_1;\ Q_2/Q_1=T_2/T_1\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Temperature at which the rms speed of hydrogen equals the Earth's escape speed, comparison of rms speeds of different gases, and why light gases escape from planetary atmospheres
questions.question: At what temperature would the rms speed of H₂ molecules (\(M=2.0\times10^{-3}\) kg/mol) equal the escape speed from the Earth, 11.2 km/s (\(R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\))? Which statement is correct?
options: A) About 100 K; hydrogen is retained because its rms speed is small
B) About \(1.0\times10^6\) K; oxygen escapes faster than hydrogen
C) About 300 K, the temperature of the atmosphere

D) \(T=\dfrac{Mv^2}{3R}\approx1.0\times10^4\) K; at 300 K the rms speed of H₂ is about 1.9 km/s, far below 11.2 km/s, yet hydrogen has been lost from the atmosphere because a fraction of molecules in the tail of the speed distribution exceed escape speed; oxygen would need 16 times the temperature to match the rms speed of hydrogen
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(T\approx1.0\times10^4\) K; \(v_{\text{rms}}(\text{H}_2,300\ \mathrm K)\approx1.9\) km/s; fast tail escapes; O₂ needs \(16\times\) the temperature.
Given: \(M=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/mol},\ v=1.12\times10^4\ \mathrm{m/s}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}\Rightarrow T=\dfrac{Mv^2}{3R}\)
Step 1: \(T=\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-3}\times(1.12\times10^4)^2}{3\times8.314}=\dfrac{2.509\times10^5}{24.94}\)
Step 2: \(T\approx1.01\times10^4\ \mathrm K\)
Step 3: \(v_{\text{rms}}(300\ \mathrm K)=\sqrt{\dfrac{3\times8.314\times300}{2.0\times10^{-3}}}=\sqrt{3.74\times10^6}=1.93\times10^3\ \mathrm{m/s}\)
Worked derivation: \[v_{\text{rms}}\propto\sqrt{T/M}:\ \frac{T_{\text{O}_2}}{T_{\text{H}_2}}=\frac{M_{\text{O}_2}}{M_{\text{H}_2}}=16\]
Check: \[\frac{11.2}{1.93}=5.8;\ 5.8^2\approx33.6;\ 300\times33.6\approx1.0\times10^4\ \mathrm K\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the Maxwell distribution has a long high-speed tail, so over geological time even gases with }v_{\text{rms}}\text{ well below escape speed leak away, the lightest fastest}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{far too low}\); (B) \(\text{factor 100 error; lighter gases escape more easily}\); (C) \(\text{at 300 K }v_{\text{rms}}\approx1.9\text{ km/s}\).
Key point: \(v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{3RT/M};\ \text{light gases escape via the fast tail}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Measuring g with a simple pendulum by timing many oscillations, the T² versus L graph and its slope, and the effect of measuring length to the top of the bob
questions.question: A student times 20 oscillations of a simple pendulum of effective length 1.00 m (string plus bob radius) as 40.2 s, and repeats for other lengths to plot \(T^2\) against \(L\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(T=40.2\) s; \(g=0.024\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\); the graph of \(T\) against \(L\) is a straight line through the origin

B) \(T=2.01\) s, so \(g=\dfrac{4\pi^2L}{T^2}=\dfrac{39.48}{4.04}\approx9.77\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\); the \(T^2\)–\(L\) graph is a straight line through the origin with slope \(\dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}\approx4.04\ \mathrm{s^2/m}\); timing 20 oscillations reduces the reaction-time error per period; if the student measured only the string length (omitting the bob radius) the line would not pass through the origin and \(g\) from a single reading would be underestimated; small amplitudes are needed for SHM
C) The period depends on the mass of the bob, so a heavier bob gives a larger \(g\)
D) The slope of the \(T^2\)–\(L\) graph equals \(g\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(T=2.01\) s; \(g\approx9.77\) m/s²; slope \(4\pi^2/g\).
Given: \(L=1.00\ \mathrm m;\ 20T=40.2\ \mathrm s\)
Formula/Principle: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac Lg}\Rightarrow T^2=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}L\)
Step 1: \(T=\dfrac{40.2}{20}=2.01\ \mathrm s;\ T^2=4.04\ \mathrm{s^2}\)
Step 2: \(g=\dfrac{4\pi^2\times1.00}{4.04}=\dfrac{39.48}{4.04}=9.77\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\)
Step 3: \(\text{slope}=\dfrac{T^2}{L}=4.04\ \mathrm{s^2/m}\Rightarrow g=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{\text{slope}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{using string length }l=L-r:\ T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{g}(l+r)\Rightarrow\text{intercept }-r\text{ on the }l\text{ axis; } g_{\text{single}}=\frac{4\pi^2l}{T^2}<g\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\frac{\mathrm m}{\mathrm s^2}\ \checkmark;\ 9.77\text{ close to }9.8\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the period depends only on length and }g\text{ for small swings; plotting }T^2\text{ against }L\text{ linearises the relation and averages out random errors}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{20 oscillations, not one; }T\propto\sqrt L\text{ is not linear}\); (C) \(\text{period is independent of mass}\); (D) \(\text{slope is }4\pi^2/g\).
Key point: \(T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{g}L;\ \text{effective length to bob centre}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Fundamental frequency of a sonometer wire from tension, length and linear density, and how it scales when each is changed, with harmonic frequencies and node spacing
questions.question: A sonometer wire 0.80 m long with linear density \(5.0\times10^{-3}\) kg/m is under a tension of 80 N. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Wave speed 16 m/s; fundamental 10 Hz; quadrupling the tension quadruples the frequency

B) Wave speed \(\sqrt{80/0.005}\approx126\ \mathrm{m/s}\); fundamental \(f_1=\dfrac{v}{2L}\approx79\ \mathrm{Hz}\); quadrupling the tension or halving the length doubles \(f_1\); a wire of four times the linear density needs four times the tension to give the same \(f_1\); the third harmonic is about 237 Hz, with adjacent nodes \(\lambda/2\approx0.27\) m apart
C) Fundamental 158 Hz, since \(f_1=v/L\)
D) Halving the length halves the fundamental frequency
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(v\approx126\) m/s; \(f_1\approx79\) Hz; scaling as stated; \(f_3\approx237\) Hz.
Given: \(L=0.80\ \mathrm m,\ \mu=5.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/m},\ T=80\ \mathrm N\)
Formula/Principle: \(v=\sqrt{T/\mu};\ f_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L}=\dfrac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac T\mu}\)
Step 1: \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{80}{0.005}}=\sqrt{16000}=126.5\ \mathrm{m/s}\)
Step 2: \(f_1=\dfrac{126.5}{1.60}=79.1\ \mathrm{Hz}\)
